sections.text: Balanced orthogonal designs give the same result under all three types. Differences appear mainly in unbalanced designs and models containing interactions. SS type What it tests Order-dependent? Use and caution Type I (sequential) Each term after the terms entered before it Yes Useful for hierarchical or deliberately ordered models; dangerous when order is arbitrary. Type II Each main effect adjusted for other main effects, generally not for interactions containing it No Useful for additive models without meaningful interactions. Type III Each term adjusted for every other term in the model No Common in unbalanced factorial models; interpretation depends on coding and model hierarchy. Never choose an SS type only because it produces a smaller p-value. State the model, coding, balance and scientific estimand. Excel's ToolPak does not offer a Type I/II/III choice; use GLM software for unbalanced complex designs.

sections.text: What to check, why it matters and what to do when it fails Assumption How to assess it Why it matters Remedy Independence Study design, randomization, sampling sequence, subject IDs Correlation among observations invalidates the standard error and F-test Use repeated-measures, blocking, mixed models or time-series methods Residual normality Residual Q–Q plot; histogram; Shapiro–Wilk as supporting evidence Especially important with small or highly unbalanced groups Investigate data errors/outliers; transform; robust or permutation method Equal variances Residuals versus fits; group SDs; Levene or Brown–Forsythe test Classical pooled MSE can be misleading when imbalance and heteroscedasticity combine Welch ANOVA; Games–Howell; transformation; robust model No influential outliers Boxplots, standardized residuals, leverage and influence Squared deviations make ANOVA sensitive to extreme points Correct errors; investigate special causes; justify robust sensitivity analysis Sphericity (repeated measures) Mauchly's test plus covariance inspection Standard univariate repeated-measures F-tests assume equal variances of pairwise differences Greenhouse–Geisser/Huynh–Feldt correction or mixed model Homogeneous regression slopes (ANCOVA) Preliminary Factor×Covariate interaction A single adjusted group difference is misleading when slopes differ Model the interaction or report group-specific slopes Equal covariance matrices (MANOVA/MANCOVA) Box's M with graphical/robust judgment Multivariate test behavior depends on group covariance structure Prefer Pillai's trace; robust analysis; reconsider outcomes/model Do not use assumption tests mechanically. A large sample can make a trivial departure “significant,” while a small sample can miss a serious departure. Combine design knowledge, residual plots, group sizes and sensitivity analyses. sections.heading: Does cooling strategy change yield strength?
breadcrumb: ANOVA Analysis: The Complete One-Stop Masterclass
Does cooling strategy change yield strength?
sections.text: An engineer compares three cooling strategies using five independently produced coils per strategy. The response is yield strength in MPa. Coil Standard Moderate Intensive 1 472 490 508 2 478 495 512 3 475 488 505 4 469 492 510 5 476 497 515 State the hypotheses. H₀: μ Standard = μ Moderate = μ Intensive . H₁: at least one differs. Compute group means. Standard = 474.0 MPa; Moderate = 492.4 MPa; Intensive = 510.0 MPa. Grand mean = 492.13 MPa. Compute between-group SS. 5(474−492.13)² + 5(492.4−492.13)² + 5(510−492.13)² = 3240.53. Compute within-group SS. Sum the squared deviations from each group mean: 50.0 + 53.2 + 58.0 = 161.2. Check the identity. SS Total = 3401.73 = 3240.53 + 161.20. Convert SS to MS. df B = 2, df W = 12. MS B = 1620.27; MS W = 13.43. Calculate F. F = 1620.27 / 13.43 = 120.62. Decide and interpret. p is far below 0.05, so reject H₀. Cooling strategy is associated with yield strength. Follow with multiplicity-controlled comparisons and effect size. Practical reading: the means increase by about 18 MPa at each step, while within-strategy standard deviations are only about 3–4 MPa. The signal is large relative to noise. Interactive calculator

breadcrumb: ANOVA Analysis: The Complete One-Stop Masterclass

sections.text: Method: two-way factorial ANOVA with replication. Factor A is setup (A/B/C); factor B is shift (day/night); response is OD deviation. Four coils replicate every setup×shift cell. Hypotheses: (1) setup main effect: marginal setup means are equal; (2) shift main effect: day and night marginal means are equal; (3) setup×shift interaction: the shift effect is the same for all setups. Predicted pattern: Setup C deteriorates much more on night shift than A or B, so non-parallel lines and a likely interaction are expected. Interpret simple setup effects within each shift and the shift effect within each setup. Excel: Data → Data Analysis → ANOVA: Two-Factor With Replication, with Rows per sample = 4 after arranging the balanced blocks correctly. Diagnostics: independence from the run/sampling plan, residual normal probability plot, residuals versus fitted values, group variance comparison, unusual residuals/outliers, and whether time order or coil sequence suggests drift. Final summary

sections.heading: Eight takeaways
breadcrumb: ANOVA Analysis: The Complete One-Stop Masterclass
sections.text: Start with the design, not the software menu. ANOVA compares explained variation with residual variation. A significant omnibus result means at least one effect exists—not that every group differs. Independence is designed into the study; it cannot be repaired by a normality test. Use Welch/Games–Howell when unequal variances and imbalance threaten classical ANOVA. Interpret interactions before main effects. Use effect size, intervals and operational criteria alongside p-values. Excel covers three layouts; advanced designs require GLM, mixed or multivariate software.

sections.heading: 1. Big idea
sections.text: A goodness-of-fit test answers one question: does the observed distribution fit the expected distribution?
sections.excerpt: A goodness-of-fit test answers one question: does the observed distribution fit the expected distribution?

sections.heading: Observed counts
sections.text: These are the actual counts you collected from the sample. Example: 35 scratches, 20 dents, 30 cracks, 15 wrong-size defects.
sections.excerpt: These are the actual counts you collected from the sample. Example: 35 scratches, 20 dents, 30 cracks, 15 wrong-size defects.

sections.heading: Expected counts
sections.text: These are the counts you would expect if the null hypothesis were true. If each of 4 defect types should be equally likely and n = 100, each expected count is 25.
sections.excerpt: These are the counts you would expect if the null hypothesis were true. If each of 4 defect types should be equally likely and n = 100, each expected count is 25.

sections.heading: Decision
sections.text: If the observed counts are too far from the expected counts, reject the null hypothesis. This test is right-tailed because only large χ² values show poor fit.
sections.excerpt: If the observed counts are too far from the expected counts, reject the null hypothesis. This test is right-tailed because only large χ² values show poor fit.

sections.heading: Specified probabilities
breadcrumb: 4. Degrees of freedom: specified vs estimated probabilities
sections.text: The expected probabilities are given before the sample is analyzed. You do not estimate any distribution parameter from the sample. Formula: df = k − 1 Example: A fair die has six specified probabilities: 1/6 for each side. Since k = 6, df = 6 − 1 = 5.

sections.text: A factory expects four defect types to occur equally often. A sample of 100 defects gives the counts below.

sections.heading: Problem data
sections.text: Defect type Observed Expected p Scratch 35 0.25 Dent 20 0.25 Crack 30 0.25 Wrong size 15 0.25 Use α = 0.05.
sections.excerpt: Defect type Observed Expected p Scratch 35 0.25 Dent 20 0.25 Crack 30 0.25 Wrong size 15 0.25 Use α = 0.05.

sections.heading: Reveal the solution
sections.text: 1 Hypotheses H₀: the four defect types occur equally often. H₁: the defect types do not occur equally often. 2 Expected counts n = 100 and p = 0.25 for each category. Therefore, E = 100 × 0.25 = 25 for each category. 3 χ² statistic χ² = (35−25)²/25 + (20−25)²/25 + (30−25)²/25 + (15−25)²/25 = 10.00. 4 Degrees of freedom There are k = 4 categories and no estimated parameters. df = k − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3. 5 Conclusion For df = 3 and α = 0.05, the critical value is about 7.815. Since 10.00 > 7.815, reject H₀. The defect pattern is significantly different from equal proportions.

lessons.title: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
lessons.description: Master the bell curve, the 68-95-99.7 rule, and z-scores with interactive graphs, a live calculator, worked examples, and a quiz.
keywords: normal distribution bell curve gaussian empirical rule 68 95 99.7 z score standard deviation probability percentile statistics basics beginner interactive calculator

sections.heading: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
sections.text: Statistics Beginner 15 minutes Interactive The normal distribution — the famous “bell curve” — describes how many real-world measurements naturally spread around an average. In this lesson you’ll learn to read the curve, use the 68–95–99.7 rule, and turn any measurement into a z-score you can interpret in seconds. Why this matters: heights, exam marks, measurement errors, filling volumes, cycle times — a huge amount of workplace data is roughly bell-shaped. Once you can read that shape, you can answer questions like “how unusual is this result?” without ever opening a statistics textbook.

breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve

Explain what the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) control in a bell curve. Apply the 68–95–99.7 rule to estimate what proportion of data falls in a given range. Calculate a z-score for any measurement and interpret what it means. Select situations where the normal model is (and is not) a sensible assumption.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
sections.text: You should be comfortable with the idea of an average (mean) and basic arithmetic (subtraction and division). That’s it. If you have met the standard deviation before, great — but we recap it below, so no prior statistics knowledge is required.
sections.excerpt: You should be comfortable with the idea of an average (mean) and basic arithmetic (subtraction and division). That’s it. If you have met the standard deviation before, great — but we recap it below, so no prior statistics knowledge is required.

sections.heading: The idea in plain English
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
sections.text: Measure the height of 1,000 adults and draw a bar chart of the results. You won’t get a random mess — you’ll get a very particular shape: most people are close to the average, and the further you move from the average, the fewer people you find. The result is a smooth, symmetric hill: the bell curve. What it is: the normal (or Gaussian) distribution is a mathematical model for data that clusters symmetrically around an average. It is completely described by just two numbers: the mean (where the centre is) and the standard deviation (how spread out the data is). Why it is used: it shows up everywhere. When a result is the sum of many small, independent influences — genetics plus diet plus environment for height, or dozens of tiny process variations for a machined part — the combined outcome tends to be bell-shaped. This is why heights, exam marks, measurement errors, IQ scores, and daily temperatures all look roughly normal. What question it answers: “How common or unusual is a particular value?” If you know the mean and standard deviation, the curve tells you what fraction of results you should expect in any range. Where it is used in practice: quality control limits, grading and performance comparisons, tolerance and specification analysis, forecasting error bands, and as the foundation of most classic statistical tests. What it does not tell us: the normal curve is a model , not a law of nature. Plenty of real data is not normal — incomes, house prices, call-waiting times, and defect counts are usually lopsided (skewed). Assuming normality without checking is one of the most common mistakes in data analysis, and we’ll show you how to spot it. Only the middle curve “behaves normally.” Skewed data needs different tools — don’t force the bell curve onto it.

sections.heading: Key terminology
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
sections.text: Terms you’ll meet in this lesson Term Plain-language meaning Technical meaning Practical interpretation Mean (μ) The average. The balance point of the distribution; for a normal curve it sits exactly at the peak. “A typical value.” Slide μ and the whole curve moves left or right. Standard deviation (σ) A typical distance from the average. The square root of the variance; the distance from the mean to the curve’s inflection point. Small σ = tall, narrow curve (consistent data). Large σ = short, wide curve (variable data). Normal / Gaussian distribution The bell curve. A continuous, symmetric distribution fully defined by μ and σ. A model for data where values cluster evenly around an average. z-score How many standard deviations a value is from the mean. z = (x − μ) / σ; a value from the standard normal distribution (μ = 0, σ = 1). z = +2 means “unusually high”; z = 0 means “perfectly average.” Empirical rule The 68–95–99.7 shortcut. For normal data: about 68% of values lie within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ. Lets you estimate proportions instantly, with no tables or software. Skewness Lopsidedness. Asymmetry of a distribution; a long tail on one side. A warning sign that the normal model (and the empirical rule) may not apply. Percentile The share of values below a given point. The cumulative probability up to a value. “90th percentile” = higher than about 90% of results.
sections.excerpt: Terms you’ll meet in this lesson Term Plain-language meaning Technical meaning Practical interpretation Mean (μ) The average. The balance point of the distribution; for a normal curve it sits exactly at the peak. “A typical value.” Slide μ and the whole curve…

sections.heading: The formula (gently)
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
sections.text: You will rarely compute this by hand — software does it for you — but seeing it once removes the mystery. The height of the bell curve at any value x is: f ( x ) = 1 σ√ 2π · e −( x − μ)² / 2σ² f(x) the height (density) of the curve at value x — taller means “more likely around here” μ the mean of the data (same units as x , e.g. cm, marks, ml) σ the standard deviation of the data (same units as x ; must be greater than 0) π the constant pi ≈ 3.14159 e Euler’s number ≈ 2.71828 Plain-language interpretation: the exponent measures how far x is from the mean, in units of σ. Values close to μ get a small exponent and a tall curve; values far from μ get a large negative exponent and the curve drops toward zero. The fraction at the front simply scales the curve so the total area underneath equals 1 (i.e. 100% of the data). Assumptions — use this model when: the data is continuous (or nearly so), roughly symmetric with one peak, and free of hard boundaries near the bulk of the data. Do not use it when: the data is clearly skewed (incomes, waiting times), is a count of rare events (defects per unit), has two peaks (mixed populations), or is capped hard at a boundary (e.g. percentages piling up at 0% or 100%).

sections.heading: The one formula you will use: the z-score
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
The one formula you will use: the z-score
sections.text: z = x − μ σ z the z-score: distance from the mean, measured in standard deviations (no units) x the value you are examining (in original units) μ the mean; σ the standard deviation (σ > 0) Plain-language interpretation: subtract the average, then divide by the “typical distance.” The answer tells you how many typical distances your value sits above (+) or below (−) the mean. Standardising like this lets you compare apples with oranges: a z-score of +1.5 on an exam means the same “degree of unusualness” as a z-score of +1.5 in height.

sections.heading: The 68–95–99.7 rule
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
sections.text: Here is the superpower of the normal distribution. For any normal data, no matter the mean or standard deviation: About 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean (34.1% on each side). About 95% fall within 2 standard deviations (adding 13.6% on each side). About 99.7% fall within 3 standard deviations (adding 2.1% on each side, leaving roughly 0.1% in each extreme tail). The empirical rule. Memorise 68 / 95 / 99.7 and you can estimate proportions for any normal dataset in your head. Instant example: adult heights with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. Then about 68% of people are between 162 and 178 cm, about 95% are between 154 and 186 cm, and only about 0.15% are taller than 194 cm (that’s beyond +3σ).

Mean μ: 100 Standard deviation σ: 15 With mean 100 and standard deviation 15 , about 68% of values fall between 85 and 115 , and about 95% fall between 70 and 130 . sections.heading: Step-by-step: answering “how unusual is this value?”
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
Step-by-step: answering “how unusual is this value?”
sections.text: Check the shape first. Plot a histogram (or dot plot) of your data. You are looking for one peak and rough symmetry. If it’s clearly skewed or has two peaks, stop — the normal model doesn’t apply. Find the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ). From your data, from software, or from a known specification. Choose your tool. If the value of interest sits neatly at ±1, 2, or 3σ, the empirical rule is enough. Otherwise, compute a z-score. Calculate. z = (x − μ) / σ. Keep the sign: negative means below the mean. Convert to a proportion. Use the empirical rule, a z-table, or software (Excel’s NORM.S.DIST ) to turn z into “% of values below/above this point.” Interpret in context. Translate back to plain language: “a fill volume of 372 ml is 2.2 standard deviations above target — fewer than 2 bottles in 100 should be this full.” Document. Record the mean, standard deviation, sample size, and the date/source of the data, so the analysis can be checked and repeated.

sections.heading: Worked example: is this exam score exceptional?
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
Worked example: is this exam score exceptional?
sections.text: The problem: a certification exam has scores that are approximately normally distributed. Priya scored 88 . Her team lead asks: “How good is that, really?” The data: historical results show a mean of μ = 72 marks and a standard deviation of σ = 8 marks. The histogram of past scores is single-peaked and symmetric, so the normal model is reasonable. The method: standardise the score with a z-score, then use the empirical rule. The formula: z = x − μ σ Substitute the values: z = 88 − 72 8 Intermediate calculation: the numerator is 88 − 72 = 16 . Then 16 ÷ 8 = 2 . Final answer: z = +2.0 — Priya’s score is exactly 2 standard deviations above the mean. Practical interpretation: by the empirical rule, 95% of scores fall within ±2σ of the mean, so 5% fall outside — and by symmetry, half of that 5% (about 2.5% ) is above +2σ. Priya beat roughly 97.5% of past candidates. That is a genuinely exceptional result, and you worked it out with nothing but subtraction, division, and one memorised rule. Limitations: this assumes past scores really are close to normal and that the historical mean and standard deviation still describe current exams. If the exam changed recently, the comparison is weaker.

sections.text: When you see this, it means this When you see… It means… z = 0 The value is exactly average. z between −1 and +1 Completely ordinary — about 68% of all values live here. z beyond ±2 Unusual — only about 5% of values are this far from the mean. Worth a closer look. z beyond ±3 Rare (about 0.3%). In quality control this typically triggers an out-of-control signal. A histogram with one peak and mirror-image sides The normal model is plausible; the empirical rule should work well. Mean noticeably larger than the median Right skew — a long tail of high values. Be cautious with the normal model. Data piled up against a boundary (e.g. 0) Likely skewed; the bell curve would predict impossible negative values. Two separate peaks Probably two mixed groups (two machines, two shifts). Split the data before modelling.

1. Assuming everything is normal Assumption error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: many datasets (incomes, waiting times, defect counts) are skewed, so normal-based percentages will be badly off. How to avoid it: always compute x − μ carefully and keep the sign through the whole calculation.

sections.heading: Practice activity: the bottling line
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
sections.text: Scenario: a bottling machine fills juice bottles with a mean of μ = 350 ml and a standard deviation of σ = 10 ml . Historical fill volumes are approximately normal. Your task: using only the empirical rule (no calculator needed), answer: What percentage of bottles contain between 340 ml and 360 ml ? What percentage of bottles contain more than 370 ml ? The legal minimum on the label is 320 ml . Roughly how often should a bottle fall below it? Work each one out (a quick sketch of the curve helps), then check yourself. 1. About 68%. 340 and 360 are exactly μ − 1σ and μ + 1σ (350 − 10 and 350 + 10). The empirical rule says about 68% of values fall within ±1σ. 2. About 2.5%. 370 = 350 + 2×10 = μ + 2σ. About 95% of bottles fall within ±2σ, leaving 5% outside. The curve is symmetric, so half of that 5% — about 2.5% — is above +2σ. 3. Almost never — about 0.1–0.15% of bottles. 320 = 350 − 3×10 = μ − 3σ. About 99.7% of bottles fall within ±3σ, leaving 0.3% outside, split between two tails. Below −3σ is roughly 0.15% — about 1 or 2 bottles in every 1,000. The reasoning pattern: convert each boundary into “how many σ from μ?”, then read the proportion straight off the 68–95–99.7 rule, remembering to halve any leftover percentage when the question asks about one tail only.

sections.heading: Key takeaways
breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
sections.text: The normal distribution is a symmetric, single-peaked model where values cluster around the mean. Two numbers describe it completely: the mean μ (location) and the standard deviation σ (spread). The empirical rule: about 68% of values fall within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ. A z-score, z = (x − μ) / σ, converts any value into “standard deviations from the mean” so different measurements can be compared fairly. |z| beyond 2 is unusual; |z| beyond 3 is rare and usually worth investigating. Software gives the area below a value by default — subtract from 100% when you need the area above. Always plot your data first: skewed, bounded, or two-peaked data breaks the normal model.

breadcrumb: The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve
sections.text: If the histogram shows one peak and rough symmetry , use the normal model: boundaries at whole multiples of σ → empirical rule; anything else → z-score plus a table or software. If the histogram is skewed, bounded, or two-peaked , do not use the normal model. Remember this: subtract the mean, divide by σ — then let 68–95–99.7 do the talking. lessons.title: Resampling in Minitab
lessons.description: Learn bootstrap confidence intervals and randomization tests through five guided Minitab labs, editable datasets, live simulations, and coached interpretation.
keywords: resampling bootstrap randomization test permutation test confidence interval p value minitab excel simulation statistics beginner interactive

sections.heading: 1. Begin with the big idea
sections.text: Resampling means repeatedly rebuilding samples with a computer. We use the patterns in those rebuilt samples to measure uncertainty or test a claim when a textbook distribution is not our best starting point.
sections.excerpt: Resampling means repeatedly rebuilding samples with a computer. We use the patterns in those rebuilt samples to measure uncertainty or test a claim when a textbook distribution is not our best starting point.

sections.heading: Let us slow that sentence down
breadcrumb: Let us slow that sentence down
sections.text: You normally have one real sample : perhaps 120 tensile-strength results, 40 customer wait times, or 25 fill weights from a packaging line. That sample gives one mean, one median, or one pass rate. The uncomfortable question is: if we collected another reasonable sample from the same process, how much might the answer move? Collecting thousands of new physical samples would be slow, expensive, and—if your test destroys the specimen—a little hard on the budget. Resampling lets the computer create many rehearsal samples from the evidence already available. It calculates the statistic for each rehearsal, then studies how those answers vary. Think of it as letting your dataset audition for the same role thousands of times. Some rows appear repeatedly; some miss a particular audition. The computer is fast, does not ask for overtime, and never complains about running sample number 9,999.

Why not always use a textbook curve?
sections.text: Classical formulas are excellent when their assumptions fit. Resampling is especially helpful for awkward statistics, questionable normality, or when seeing the simulated logic makes the uncertainty easier to understand. Important reality check: “Computer-generated sample” does not mean “new evidence.” If every thermometer was miscalibrated by 3°C, resampling will reproduce the mistake thousands of times—with impressive speed and absolutely no shame. The original sample still must be representative, measured correctly, and collected with the right sampling unit.

sections.heading: Bootstrap and randomization are cousins, not twins
breadcrumb: Bootstrap and randomization are cousins, not twins
sections.text: Bootstrap → estimation Ask: “What values are plausible for the population mean or mean difference?” Output: confidence interval. Randomization → hypothesis testing Ask: “If the null claim were true, how often would a result this extreme occur?” Output: p-value. Data → apply resampling rule → calculate statistic → repeat many times → interpret distribution Questions & Answers — 21 questions Open this section to explore common questions about bootstrapping and randomization tests. What does “with replacement” mean? After a row is drawn, it goes back into the pool before the next draw. A row can appear zero, one, or several times. The resample stays the same size as the original sample. Does resampling create new real-world information? No. It reveals what the observed data imply under a specific resampling rule. A biased, dependent, or unrepresentative sample remains problematic. Does a confidence interval assume that the underlying distribution is normal? Not always. It depends on what confidence interval you are calculating, the sample size, and the method used . Situation Does the raw data need to be normal? Why? Small sample, for example n < 30 Approximately yes for a classical t-based interval The method relies more heavily on the population being approximately normal. Large sample, for example n ≥ 30 Usually no The Central Limit Theorem often makes the sampling distribution of the mean approximately normal. Very skewed data or major outliers Be careful Even n = 30 may not be enough. Bootstrap confidence interval No normality assumption is required The sampling distribution is estimated by resampling the observed data. The key distinction is that a standard confidence interval for the mean does not necessarily require the raw data to be normally distributed . What matters is whether the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal. For example, individual Charpy values could be right-skewed: 80, 95, 110, 115, 125, 140, 160, 220, 310, … If you repeatedly took samples of 50 specimens and calculated the mean of each sample, those means would tend to form a more nearly normal distribution because of the Central Limit Theorem. Keep the two distributions separate: Population or data distribution → can be non-normal. Sampling distribution of x̄ → becomes approximately normal as n increases. Important: “ n ≥ 30” is a rule of thumb, not a law. Severe skewness or outliers may require a much larger sample or a bootstrap interval. What is the difference between randomization and bootstrapping? Randomization asks: “Could this observed difference have happened by chance if there were really no effect?” Bootstrapping asks: “How uncertain is my estimate?” Suppose two rolling practices have an observed mean Charpy difference of about 31 J. Randomization or permutation test: start with the null hypothesis that the two groups are equivalent. Combine the observations, shuffle the A/B labels, split them back into groups of the original sizes, calculate the mean difference, and repeat thousands of times. This creates a null distribution . Bootstrapping: preserve the groups and repeatedly sample with replacement from each group. Calculate the statistic each time. This creates a bootstrap distribution that describes the precision and uncertainty of the estimate. Feature Randomization Bootstrapping Main purpose Hypothesis testing Estimation and uncertainty Typical output p-value Confidence interval or standard error Main question Could this happen by chance under H₀? How variable is my estimate? Sampling Usually without replacement With replacement Group labels Usually shuffled Usually preserved Creates Null distribution Sampling distribution Memory trick: Randomization = shuffle; bootstrap = resample with replacement. Randomization asks about evidence of an effect. Bootstrap asks how precisely the effect was estimated. What does “randomization rearranges labels without replacement” mean? Suppose the observed data are: Practice A Practice B 200 150 210 160 220 170 The observed difference in means is 50 J. The randomization test asks: if A and B really had no effect, could a 50 J difference arise just by randomly assigning these observations to two groups? First remove the labels: 200, 210, 220, 150, 160, 170 Then randomly assign three observations to A and three to B. Every original observation appears exactly once in that randomization. Valid: A = [200, 160, 170] B = [210, 220, 150] Not valid: A = [200, 200, 170] The second assignment is invalid because the original dataset contained only one 200 J observation. Without replacement means that once an observation is assigned during one randomization, it cannot be selected again in that same randomization. Bootstrap sampling is different: repeated values are allowed. How do we determine how often random shuffling produces a difference as large as the observed 31 J? Begin with the observed difference: D observed = 31 J Assume the null hypothesis is true: H₀: μ A = μ B Shuffle the group labels thousands of times. After each shuffle, calculate: D* = x̄ A * − x̄ B * For a two-sided test, count randomized differences at least as extreme as the observed result in either direction: |D*| ≥ |D observed | Suppose 10,000 randomizations produce: Result Number of randomizations −31 < D* < +31 9,720 D* ≥ +31 145 D* ≤ −31 135 Total 10,000 Extreme results = 145 + 135 = 280 p = 280 / 10,000 = 0.028 If A and B truly had no difference, about 2.8% of random label assignments produced a difference at least as extreme as the 31 J result observed. Actual data → observed difference → assume H₀ → shuffle labels → calculate D* → count extreme values → p-value What about a one-sample randomization test? A one-sample randomization test follows the same broad idea, but there are no A/B group labels to shuffle. Suppose: H₀: μ = 180 J Sample: 185, 190, 175, 200, 195 The sample mean is 189 J, so the observed difference from the null value is 9 J. One possible one-sample method is a sign-randomization test . First calculate the deviations from 180: +5, +10, −5, +20, +15 Keep the magnitudes but randomly flip their signs. For example: +5, −10, +5, −20, +15 This randomized set has a mean deviation of −1 J, corresponding to a randomized sample mean of 179 J. Repeating the sign randomization creates a null distribution centered around the hypothesized value. Technical caveat: sign-flipping is not a completely assumption-free test of the population mean. It relies on an appropriate symmetry or exchangeability assumption. Minitab’s one-sample randomization procedure uses the null-centering method explained below instead. If we use the same one sample without replacement, wouldn’t the mean stay the same? Yes. That objection is correct. If we simply reorder: 185, 190, 175, 200, 195 into: 200, 175, 195, 185, 190 the mean does not change. Reordering one sample cannot create a useful null distribution. A one-sample randomization procedure must randomize something other than the observation order. In a sign-randomization approach, the signs attached to the deviation magnitudes change. For example, the magnitudes 5, 10, 5, 20, and 15 could become: +5, −10, +5, −20, +15 −5, +10, −5, +20, +15 Those different sign patterns produce different means. Key insight: If you literally shuffle a single sample without replacement, nothing happens to its mean. Is sign-flipping the method Minitab uses for a 1-sample randomization test? No. Minitab uses a different approach. Sample: 185, 190, 175, 200, 195 x̄ = 189 H₀: μ = 180 Minitab first shifts every observation by the same amount so the adjusted sample mean equals the hypothesized mean. The required shift is: 180 − 189 = −9 The null-adjusted data become: 176, 181, 166, 191, 186 adjusted mean = 180 Minitab then repeatedly resamples with replacement from this null-adjusted sample, keeping the original sample size. Each resample produces a new mean, building a null distribution centered around 180. 176, 176, 191, 181, 191 → mean = 183 166, 181, 166, 186, 176 → mean = 175 Bootstrap confidence interval Minitab 1-sample randomization Starts with the original data Starts with the original data Keeps the center at x̄ Shifts the data so the center equals μ₀ Samples with replacement Samples with replacement Builds a distribution around x̄ Builds a distribution around μ₀ Estimates uncertainty or a confidence interval Tests H₀ and calculates a p-value In short, Minitab uses bootstrap-style resampling after first forcing the data to represent the null hypothesis . How does Minitab perform a 2-sample randomization test? Minitab’s 2-sample randomization test follows the classic permutation logic. Suppose: Practice A Practice B 210 175 195 182 220 168 205 190 215 177 x̄ A = 209 x̄ B = 178.4 D observed = 30.6 J H₀: μ A − μ B = 0 Minitab pools all observations, randomly reallocates them into two groups while preserving the original group sizes, and calculates a new difference in means. Randomized A Randomized B 210 195 175 220 182 205 190 215 177 168 D* = x̄ A * − x̄ B * Repeating this process thousands of times creates a distribution centered near zero, representing differences expected under the null hypothesis. For a two-sided test, Minitab counts the proportion satisfying: |D*| ≥ 30.6 That proportion is the randomization p-value. If my original bootstrap sample size is 6 and I resample 1,000 times, does every resample also contain 6 observations? Yes. In ordinary nonparametric bootstrapping, if the original sample size is n = 6, every bootstrap resample also contains six observations. Those observations are selected with replacement . Original sample: [100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150] Sample Six selected observations Mean Original 100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150 125.0 Bootstrap #1 100, 100, 120, 140, 140, 150 125.0 Bootstrap #2 110, 110, 110, 130, 150, 150 126.7 Bootstrap #3 100, 120, 120, 120, 130, 140 121.7 Every resample contains exactly six selections, but some original observations may appear several times while others may not appear at all. Do not confuse these numbers: n = 6 → observations inside each bootstrap resample B = 1,000 → number of separate bootstrap resamples You create 1,000 separate samples of six observations each and usually calculate one statistic from each sample. Keeping the resample size at six approximates how the statistic would vary across repeated studies having the same sample size as the original study. Original sample n = 6 → draw 6 values with replacement → calculate one statistic → repeat 1,000 times → 1,000 bootstrap statistics What resampling methods should I practice in Minitab, and what questions do they answer? The practice set was organized around five Minitab resampling methods: Method Practice Variable(s) Core Question Bootstrapping for 1-Sample Function Strength_MPa What is the 95% confidence interval for the average strength? Bootstrapping for 2-Sample Means Strength_MPa + Group Is the New process mean higher than Standard? Randomization Test for 1-Sample Mean Strength_MPa Is the average strength different from 51 MPa? Randomization Test for 1-Sample Proportion PassFail Is the pass rate greater than 90%? Randomization Test for 2-Sample Means Strength_MPa + Group Is the New process statistically different from Standard? Use 1,000 or 5,000 resamples to start. Higher numbers of resamples give smoother resampling distributions. What does each resampling method mean, what is it used for, and what is a practical example? These methods in Minitab fall under resampling statistics . They are powerful because they do not rely as heavily on normal-distribution assumptions as many traditional t-tests and z-tests. They use repeated random sampling or simulation to estimate uncertainty, significance, or confidence intervals.

sections.heading: The p-value
sections.text: The p-value answers how unusual the observed result is under H 0 . A small p-value means the observed result is rare in the simulated null world; a large p-value means random variation could readily explain it. Statistical significance is also not the same as practical significance.

sections.heading: What Randomization Builds
sections.text: It builds the distribution of expected random variation under the null hypothesis — the null distribution . Suppose Minitab simulates 5,000 samples under: H 0 : μ = 51 and generates means such as 50.8, 51.2, 50.5, 51.7, 49.9. Most are near 51 because under H 0 , 51 is assumed true. Then compare the real mean, 53, and ask: “How often do simulated means get as far as 53?” Outcome Interpretation 53 is rare in the null distribution 53 is unusually far from 51 → evidence against H 0 . 53 is common in the null distribution Normal variation could readily explain it → insufficient evidence against H 0 . Simplest possible mental model: Target mean → “What are we testing against?” Resampling → “How much random variation should we expect around that target?” Randomization testing is basically: “Let’s pretend the target is true and simulate reality thousands of times. Does our observed result fit naturally into that simulated reality?” Are we resampling the original dataset, or are we simply simulating random samples? We are resampling the original dataset , but in a way that simulates what random samples would look like under the null hypothesis. That subtle distinction is the whole trick. sections.heading: Randomization Test

For example, suppose: Data = 53, 52, 54, 51, 55 and x̄ = 53 H 0 : μ = 51 The data are centered at 53, but under H 0 they should be centered at 51. So Minitab first transforms the data. Original Recentered 53 51 52 50 54 52 51 49 55 53 Then it repeatedly samples from the recentered data, computes means, and builds the null distribution. Bootstrap: Observed Data → Resample Directly → Estimate uncertainty 1-Sample Randomization: Observed Data → Recenter to H 0 → Resample → Test significance Extremely important insight: The randomization distribution represents what we would expect to see purely from random chance if the null hypothesis were true. What is the purpose of the recentering step in a 1-sample randomization test? The recentering step exists because: We must force the data to behave as though the null hypothesis is true. Without recentering, the simulation would still reflect your observed sample mean instead of the hypothesized mean. That would break the logic of the test.

sections.heading: First: what is this method?
sections.text: This test evaluates whether the mean of one population is reasonably consistent with a claimed value, μ₀. Unlike a confidence interval, it starts by temporarily assuming the null claim is true and asks: “Would our observed mean be unusual in that null world?”

sections.heading: Assumptions resampling does not erase
sections.text: The original observations should represent the target process or population. Ordinary row resampling assumes independence. Time series, batches, heats, coils, repeated measures, and clusters may need block or cluster resampling. Two-group label permutation requires exchangeability under H₀; major design differences or confounding can invalidate the shuffle. Very small samples cannot reveal unseen tails or modes; resampling only reuses observed information.

sections.text: Function Syntax Purpose When to use it AVERAGE =AVERAGE(number1,[number2],...) Calculates a sample or resample mean. Use for the one-sample mean and both two-sample mean procedures. MEDIAN =MEDIAN(number1,[number2],...) Calculates the middle value. Use when bootstrapping a median or another 1-sample location statistic. STDEV.S =STDEV.S(number1,[number2],...) Calculates sample standard deviation. Use to describe the original data and compare spread before interpreting a resampling result. COUNTIF =COUNTIF(range,criteria) Counts outcomes meeting a condition. Use to calculate Pass counts and observed proportions. ROWS =ROWS(array) Returns the sample size. Use so a resample automatically contains the same number of observations as the source sample. INDEX =INDEX(array,row_num,[column_num]) Returns observations at randomly generated row positions. Use with RANDARRAY to draw bootstrap samples with replacement. RANDARRAY =RANDARRAY([rows],[columns],[min],[max],[whole_number]) Generates random row positions or random sorting keys. Use to build bootstrap draws, Bernoulli trials, or shuffled labels. Results recalculate unless values are frozen. SORTBY =SORTBY(array,by_array1,[sort_order1],...) Randomly reorders labels when sorted by random keys. Use to create one permutation for a two-sample randomization test. FILTER =FILTER(array,include,[if_empty]) Returns values assigned to a selected group. Use after shuffling labels to calculate each permuted group mean. LET =LET(name1,name_value1,calculation) Names intermediate arrays inside one readable formula. Use to keep resampling formulas understandable and auditable. PERCENTILE.INC =PERCENTILE.INC(array,k) Returns a percentile from simulated statistics. Use the 0.025 and 0.975 percentiles for a two-sided 95% percentile bootstrap interval.

sections.heading: Exam Tips
sections.text: Know the resampling unit. ASQ CSSBB/CQE questions may hide dependence inside batches, heats, patients, shifts, or repeated readings. Resample the independent unit, not automatically every row. Separate estimation from testing. A bootstrap confidence interval estimates a plausible range for a parameter; a randomization test evaluates how unusual the observed statistic is under H₀ . Remember “with replacement.” Bootstrap samples can contain duplicates and omit original observations. That is expected, not a computer having a small crisis. Read the subtraction order. A positive New − Standard difference means New is higher. Reversing the order reverses the sign, although a two-sided significance conclusion is unchanged. Do not confuse significance with importance. Compare the effect with specifications, risk, cost, and the minimum practically meaningful difference before recommending action. Report reproducibility details. In real analysis, record the data source, statistic, resample count, confidence level or alpha, alternative hypothesis, and random seed.
sections.excerpt: Know the resampling unit. ASQ CSSBB/CQE questions may hide dependence inside batches, heats, patients, shifts, or repeated readings. Resample the independent unit, not automatically every row. Separate estimation from testing. A bootstrap confidence interval…

sections.heading: 6. Final workflow checklist
sections.text: Write the engineering question and define the population. Identify response type: continuous mean/function or binary proportion. Decide: estimate with a CI or test a null claim. Identify one sample or two groups; verify subtraction direction and event label. Check independence, sampling unit, representativeness, and confounding. Choose the matching Minitab procedure and alternative hypothesis before examining the p-value. Run many resamples; record the seed for reproducibility. Report the observed effect, interval or p-value, sample sizes, resample count, method, and practical meaning. Engineering reporting model: “The New process averaged 52.434 MPa versus 50.621 MPa for Standard (difference 1.813 MPa). A 5,000-resample analysis [insert CI or p-value]… This applies to the sampled process conditions; independence and group comparability were assumed.”

sections.heading: Chebyshev vs. the Empirical Rule
sections.text: Learn two different ways to describe how much data lies near the mean—and why one is a guarantee for almost any distribution while the other is a stronger approximation for bell-shaped data. Why this matters: engineers and analysts often know only a mean and standard deviation. Choosing the wrong rule can make a cautious statement look falsely precise.

Calculate Chebyshev coverage and the interval μ ± kσ. Compare Chebyshev with the 68–95–99.7 Empirical Rule. Select the appropriate rule from the information given about distribution shape. Interpret results using “at least,” “at most,” and “approximately” correctly.

sections.heading: Chebyshev's inequality
sections.text: Gives a minimum guaranteed proportion inside a symmetric interval for any distribution with a finite mean and variance—even when the shape is skewed, bimodal, or unknown.

sections.heading: The Empirical Rule
sections.text: States that approximately 68%, 95%, and 99.7% lie within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations when data are approximately normal. What neither rule tells you: neither proves a process is stable, capable, or normal. They describe spread around the mean, not conformity to specifications.

sections.text: P(|X − μ| < kσ) ≥ 1 − 1 k² Chebyshev's inside bound, valid for k > 1. Lower = μ − kσ | Upper = μ + kσ The bounds use the same units as the original measurement. Maximum outside ≤ 1 k² Inside and outside are complements: inside ≥ 1 − 1/k²; outside ≤ 1/k². Same interval, different claims. k Chebyshev minimum Empirical Rule Correct wording 1 0% useful guarantee About 68% Use the normal result only when normality is reasonable. 2 At least 75% About 95% Chebyshev guarantees; Empirical approximates. 3 At least 88.89% About 99.7% Do not call either value exact unless using the exact normal CDF. Assumptions: Chebyshev requires a finite mean and finite variance. The Empirical Rule additionally requires a distribution reasonably close to normal.

Calculate coverage. Chebyshev uses 1 − 1/k². Normal data use the Empirical Rule or exact normal probabilities. Calculate bounds. Use μ − kσ and μ + kσ. Interpret with disciplined language. Say “at least” for Chebyshev and “approximately” for the Empirical Rule. Document the assumption. State whether distribution shape was unknown, non-normal, or approximately normal.

sections.heading: Worked example: package fill weights
sections.text: Problem: A filler produces packages with mean 500 g and standard deviation 12 g. The distribution shape has not been established. What can be guaranteed within two standard deviations? Select the method. Shape is unknown, so use Chebyshev. Set k. The question says two standard deviations, so k = 2. Calculate coverage. 1 − 1/2² = 1 − 1/4 = 0.75 = 75%. Calculate bounds. 500 ± 2(12) = 500 ± 24, giving 476 g to 524 g. Interpret. At least 75% of all package weights lie between 476 g and 524 g, assuming the population has a finite mean and variance. Limitation: you cannot claim 95% unless the distribution is reasonably normal. Chebyshev's 75% is conservative; actual coverage may be higher.

sections.text: A filling process has mean 250 mL and standard deviation 4 mL. Distribution shape is unknown. Find an interval guaranteed to contain at least 90% of fills. Set 1 − 1/k² = 0.90. Then 1/k² = 0.10, so k² = 10 and k = √10 = 3.162. Bounds: 250 ± 3.162(4) = 250 ± 12.649, or approximately 237.35 mL to 262.65 mL . Conclusion: at least 90% of fills lie within this interval, assuming finite mean and variance.

sections.heading: Final summary
sections.text: Chebyshev gives a minimum guaranteed coverage for any distribution with finite mean and variance. The Empirical Rule gives approximate 68–95–99.7 coverage only for approximately normal data. Chebyshev inside coverage is 1 − 1/k² for k > 1. Numerical bounds are μ − kσ and μ + kσ. Use “at least” for Chebyshev and “approximately” for the Empirical Rule. A conservative bound can be much lower than the actual proportion. Decision rule: unknown or non-normal shape → Chebyshev; approximately normal shape → Empirical Rule or exact normal probabilities. Remember this: Chebyshev guarantees; the Empirical Rule assumes. lessons.description: Compare linear, monotonic, and rank-based association with a live relationship explorer, a concordant/discordant pairs demo, a paste-your-own-data calculator, and Excel + Minitab guidance.
keywords: pearson correlation spearman rank correlation kendall tau correlation coefficient concordant discordant pairs monotonic relationship linear relationship nonparametric correlation correlation vs causation outliers ranks excel minitab statistics intermediate interactive

sections.heading: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: When you select a correlation metric, you are fundamentally choosing how you want to measure association between two variables. The three most common coefficients — Pearson , Spearman , and Kendall — differ in their assumptions, their sensitivity to outliers and non-linearity, and exactly what number they hand you at the end. Picking the wrong one doesn't just give you an imprecise answer — it can give you a confidently wrong one. Why it matters: Reporting a Pearson r on skewed, outlier-heavy, or ranked engineering data is one of the most common statistics mistakes on the shop floor — and one of the more commonly tested distinctions on the ASQ CSSBB and CQE exams.
sections.excerpt: When you select a correlation metric, you are fundamentally choosing how you want to measure association between two variables. The three most common coefficients — Pearson , Spearman , and Kendall — differ in their assumptions, their sensitivity to outliers…

sections.heading: Three ways to measure association
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: All three coefficients return a number between −1 and +1 . A value near +1 means the variables move together strongly and positively; near −1 means they move strongly in opposite directions; near 0 means little consistent association was detected by that particular method . That last caveat is the whole lesson: the same dataset can hand you three different numbers depending on which question you asked.

sections.heading: What it measures
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: The strength of a linear relationship between two continuous variables — how tightly the points cluster around a straight line. r = Cov(X,Y) σ X σ Y Covariance of X and Y, standardized by the product of their standard deviations.

sections.text: Range: −1 to +1 Assumes a linear relationship Assumes continuous (interval/ratio) data Assumes approximate normality and homoscedasticity Highly sensitive to outliers

sections.text: +1 → perfect positive linear relationship 0 → no linear relationship detected −1 → perfect negative linear relationship Best for process variables, financial returns, and continuous engineering measurements when the scatterplot already looks like a straight line If your data are roughly normal and you already expect linearity from the physics or process — for example, temperature vs. a mechanical property — use Pearson.

breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient

sections.heading: What it measures
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: A monotonic relationship — not necessarily a straight line, just a consistent direction. Instead of correlating the raw values, Spearman first converts each variable to ranks and then runs a Pearson correlation on those ranks. ρ = 1 − 6∑d i 2 n(n 2 −1) d i is the difference between the ranks of the i-th pair of observations; n is the sample size. (This shortcut form assumes no tied ranks; with ties, Spearman is computed as the Pearson correlation of the two rank columns instead.)

breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Range: −1 to +1 Nonparametric — no normality assumption Works with ordinal data as well as continuous data Less sensitive to outliers than Pearson (an extreme value only shifts a rank, not the raw distance)
sections.excerpt: Range: −1 to +1 Nonparametric — no normality assumption Works with ordinal data as well as continuous data Less sensitive to outliers than Pearson (an extreme value only shifts a rank, not the raw distance)

sections.heading: Interpretation & when to use
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Measures whether, as X increases, Y tends to increase (or decrease) consistently Best for non-normal or skewed data, ordinal data, and monotonic-but-curved relationships If the relationship is monotonic but visibly curved — for example, a rank of defect severity vs. customer complaints — use Spearman. Rank each variable separately. The smallest X gets rank 1, the next smallest rank 2, and so on; tied values share the average of the ranks they would have occupied. Do the same for Y. Run an ordinary Pearson correlation on the two rank columns. That result is ρ.

sections.heading: What it measures
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Association based on concordant vs. discordant pairs . Take every possible pair of observations. If the pair agrees on ordering — the one with the bigger X also has the bigger Y — it's concordant . If they disagree, it's discordant . Kendall's tau is built directly from that tally. τ = C − D ½n(n−1) C = number of concordant pairs, D = number of discordant pairs. (The version used below and by most software, “tau-b,” adjusts the denominator to account for tied ranks.)

sections.heading: Practical decision rule

sections.text: Is the data continuous and roughly normal, and do you expect a straight-line relationship? → Use Pearson . Is the relationship monotonic but not linear? → Use Spearman . Is the sample small, or are there many tied ranks? → Use Kendall . Always look at the scatterplot before trusting any single number. sections.heading: Common pitfalls
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Correlation is not causation. Any of the three coefficients can be large because of a lurking (confounding) variable, not because X drives Y. A single outlier can dominate Pearson. Two extreme points can swing r dramatically while barely moving Spearman or Kendall — try the “Outliers present” preset above. Zero correlation does not mean no relationship. All three coefficients can sit near zero for a strong but non-monotonic (curved both ways) pattern. Ties need the right formula. Skip the shortcut Spearman formula when ranks are tied; use the rank-then-Pearson approach or the tau-b version of Kendall instead. A big r does not certify a good regression. Linearity, constant variance, and independence still need to be checked separately before fitting a line.

sections.heading: Excel Functions
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Functions used across this lesson's Excel workflow Function Syntax Purpose When to use it CORREL =CORREL(array1,array2) Pearson correlation coefficient between two ranges. Use directly on raw values for Pearson r; use on two rank columns to get Spearman ρ. PEARSON =PEARSON(array1,array2) Mathematically identical to CORREL ; older function name kept for compatibility. Either function is fine — most analysts default to CORREL . RSQ =RSQ(known_ys,known_xs) Returns the square of the Pearson correlation coefficient (r²). Use to report the proportion of variance explained when discussing r in a simple-linear-regression context. RANK.AVG =RANK.AVG(number,ref,[order]) Ranks a value within a range, averaging tied ranks. Use to build the rank columns that Spearman (and a manual Kendall check) both depend on. Prefer this over the legacy RANK , which does not average ties. SIGN =SIGN(number) Returns −1, 0, or +1. Use on pairwise differences to classify a pair as concordant, discordant, or tied when building Kendall's tau by hand. SUMPRODUCT =SUMPRODUCT(array1,array2,...) Multiplies arrays element-wise and sums the result. Use with SIGN across a helper pairwise grid to tally concordant/discordant pairs for Kendall's tau (Excel has no native KENDALL function). T.DIST.2T =T.DIST.2T(x,deg_freedom) Two-tailed p-value from the t-distribution. Use to test whether a Pearson r is significantly different from zero: t = r√((n−2)/(1−r²)), then =T.DIST.2T(ABS(t), n-2) . FISHER / FISHERINV =FISHER(x) / =FISHERINV(y) Fisher z-transformation and its inverse. Use to build an approximate confidence interval for Pearson r: transform r with FISHER , build a normal-based interval on the z-scale, then convert the endpoints back with FISHERINV .

sections.heading: Minitab Navigation
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Menu paths for correlation in Minitab Task Menu path Notes Pearson or Spearman correlation Stat → Basic Statistics → Correlation Enter two or more numeric columns; the dialog's Method option lets you choose Pearson (default) or Spearman rank correlation, plus a significance test for each pair. Check linearity/monotonicity first Graph → Scatterplot Alternative/companion step. Always view the scatterplot — with or without a fitted line — before trusting a correlation number, since Minitab will compute r or ρ on any pair of columns whether or not the relationship is actually well-suited to it. Kendall's tau between two variables No dedicated menu item in standard Minitab Basic Statistics Be transparent about this limitation: Minitab's built-in Correlation dialog covers Pearson and Spearman only. For a two-variable Kendall's tau, either compute it manually from ranks (as shown above) or use software with native support (e.g., R's cor(method="kendall") or Python's scipy.stats.kendalltau ). Do not confuse this with Minitab's separate Kendall's Coefficient of Concordance , which measures agreement across multiple raters and is a different statistic. Which option should you choose? Start from the decision rule, not the menu: run Stat → Basic Statistics → Correlation with Method set to Pearson when you expect linearity and normality, switch the same dialog's Method to Spearman when the relationship is monotonic but not linear or the data are ordinal, and fall back to a manual or external Kendall's tau calculation for small, tie-heavy samples.

sections.heading: Exam Tips
breadcrumb: Pearson, Spearman & Kendall: Choosing the Right Correlation Coefficient
sections.text: Correlation ≠ causation, every time it's tested. ASQ CSSBB/CQE items frequently plant a high r and ask what conclusion is defensible — the answer is rarely “X causes Y.” Match the assumption to the data before picking a formula. A question describing skewed, ordinal, or ranked engineering data (defect severity tiers, inspector scores) is cueing you toward Spearman or Kendall, not Pearson. Know why r can mislead. Exam scenarios love the “one extreme outlier” setup precisely because it shows Pearson's sensitivity — if the question hinges on a couple of unusual points, expect Spearman/Kendall to be the more defensible answer. Connect r to regression. r² (via RSQ ) is the proportion of variance in Y explained by a simple linear fit on X — a common bridge question between correlation and regression topics. Ties matter for both real analysis and exam wording. If a scenario mentions repeated or tied ranks, that's the cue for Kendall's tau-b or a rank-based Spearman calculation, not the tie-naive shortcut formula. Statistical significance is not practical significance. A statistically significant correlation in a huge dataset can still be too weak to act on; always weigh the coefficient's size against engineering tolerances and cost of action. Remember: Pearson asks “is it a straight line?”, Spearman and Kendall ask “is it a consistent direction?” — choose the question that actually matches your data before you trust the number.

sections.heading: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation
breadcrumb: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation
sections.text: Every process wobbles . Here's how to measure it. Variance, standard deviation, coefficient of variation and its cousins, covariance, and correlation are usually taught as separate formulas to memorize. They're really one idea, asked several different ways: how far do things drift from where we expect them, and do two things drift together? Drag the slider below to feel it before we name it. relationship strength: 0.70 as you drag, watch the dots snap from a cloud to a line — that snapping-into-a-line is what correlation measures. Part 1 of 6

sections.heading: CV has cousins — and each one trusts the data differently
breadcrumb: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation
CV has cousins — and each one trusts the data differently
sections.text: CV isn't the only way to express spread "relative to something." Four more live in the same family, each built from a different raw material — the full range, just the middle 50%, average distance instead of squared distance, or CV itself renamed for a lab bench. Where they disagree is how much a single wild reading can shake them . coefficient of range — spread relative to the total scale quartile coefficient of dispersion — spread of just the middle 50%, ignores the tails coefficient of mean deviation — average distance, not squared distance, relative to the average relative standard deviation — CV, renamed for the lab bench Identical math to CV — just always expressed as a percentage.

sections.heading: The clogged nozzle
breadcrumb: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation
CV has cousins — and each one trusts the data differently
sections.text: Twelve syringes off Fill Line 7, target 10.00 mL. Then the nozzle catches for one cycle and overfills a single syringe to 13.80 mL. Toggle it in and out and watch which numbers flinch. Include the clogged-nozzle syringe (13.80 mL) fill volume (mL) min / max — Q1 / Q3 — mean — mean deviation — coefficient of range — sensitive quartile coeff. of dispersion — robust coefficient of mean deviation — moderate RSD — sensitive That ordering isn't a coincidence. Quartile coefficient of dispersion only looks at Q1 and Q3 — the middle 50% of the data — so one extreme syringe usually doesn't even change which readings sit at those positions. Coefficient of mean deviation averages every distance once, so the outlier counts, but only once. Coefficient of range and RSD both key off the single most extreme reading (or its squared distance, for RSD) — exactly the reading that just broke. When to reach for which: use the quartile coefficient of dispersion when you know the data has (or might have) outliers and you don't want one bad reading to dominate the story — audits of skewed cycle-time or cost data are a classic case. Reach for RSD/CV when the data is reasonably well-behaved and you want the standard, widely-recognized metric. Coefficient of range is quick and intuitive but inherits the raw range's weakness: it only ever looks at two points. Part 4 of 6

breadcrumb: The Spread Lab: Variance, Covariance, Correlation & Coefficient of Variation
Covariance — variance's formula, aimed at two variables
sections.text: Variance multiplies each deviation by itself . Covariance multiplies the deviation of X by the deviation of a second variable, Y , at the same moment. If they tend to be above their means together (or below together), the products are positive. If one's up while the other's down, the products are negative. covariance — and variance is just this with Y = X

Every single relative measure says "pins." Both are computed correctly — they're just answering different questions. The general rule: a raw spread measure (variance, standard deviation, range, IQR, mean deviation) is only comparable between two datasets that share the same units and a similar scale. The instant you're comparing across different units, different scales, or even the same units at very different magnitudes, switch to the relative version — CV, coefficient of range, quartile coefficient of dispersion, or coefficient of mean deviation. That's the entire reason this family of measures exists. Statistics Implementation

sections.text: The formulas above are what's happening under the hood. In practice, on the exam and on the floor, you'll pull these from software — and the sample/population distinction below is the single most common place people lose points. Excel functions Function Syntax Purpose When to use VAR.S =VAR.S(range) Sample variance Your data is a sample of a larger population (the usual case) VAR.P =VAR.P(range) Population variance Your data is the entire population — no estimation involved STDEV.S =STDEV.S(range) Sample standard deviation Square root of VAR.S; the default for process/quality data STDEV.P =STDEV.P(range) Population standard deviation Square root of VAR.P AVERAGE =AVERAGE(range) Mean Needed alongside STDEV to build CV yourself — Excel has no native CV function COVARIANCE.S =COVARIANCE.S(range1,range2) Sample covariance Two paired samples (e.g. two process measurements taken together) COVARIANCE.P =COVARIANCE.P(range1,range2) Population covariance Both variables' complete populations are known CORREL =CORREL(range1,range2) Pearson correlation (r) Same result whether you treat the data as sample or population — r is scale-free either way MAX, MIN =MAX(range), =MIN(range) Extremes Build the coefficient of range yourself — no native function QUARTILE.INC =QUARTILE.INC(range,1) / (range,3) Q1 / Q3 Feeds the quartile coefficient of dispersion — again, no native function combines them for you AVEDEV =AVEDEV(range) Mean absolute deviation The numerator for coefficient of mean deviation — one of Excel's more obscure built-ins

sections.text: Sample vs. population: if the question describes measuring "all units produced" or a defined finite lot, use population formulas (n divisor). If it describes a sample pulled for inspection — the overwhelming majority of exam scenarios — use sample formulas (n−1 divisor). Using n instead of n−1 is the single most common calculation trap. Correlation ≠ causation: a classic distractor answer treats a high r as proof that X causes Y. The exam will reward "there is a strong linear association" over "X causes Y" unless the question describes a controlled experiment. CV shows up in Measurement Systems Analysis and reliability questions as a way to compare variability across different gauges or different-scaled processes — if a question compares consistency across two different units of measure, CV (not raw StDev) is almost always the intended tool.

lessons.description: See how the normal connects to the Weibull, lognormal, t, binomial and more — with a live Central Limit Theorem simulator.

sections.heading: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Statistics Intermediate 20 minutes Interactive The bell curve doesn’t live alone. It sits at the centre of a whole family of distributions — Weibull, lognormal, Student’s t, binomial, exponential — connected to it by transformations, limits, and one remarkable theorem. In this lesson you’ll simulate the Central Limit Theorem live, morph a Weibull curve into a near-bell, and learn to pick the right distribution for the job. Why this matters: real data is often not normal — failure times, repair durations, defect counts, incomes. Knowing how these distributions relate to the normal tells you when the bell-curve toolkit still applies (thanks to the Central Limit Theorem), and which specialist distribution to reach for when it doesn’t. This is core territory for Six Sigma, reliability engineering, and quality certification exams.

Select an appropriate distribution for a dataset using shape, boundaries, and data type.

sections.heading: The family map in plain English
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
The family map in plain English
sections.text: Think of the normal distribution as the busiest junction in the world of probability. Other distributions connect to it in three distinct ways: 1. Convergence — “becomes normal in the limit.” Several distributions turn into a bell curve as some quantity grows. The binomial (counts of successes in n trials) looks more and more normal as n increases. The Poisson (counts of rare events) does the same as its mean grows. Student’s t — a bell with heavier tails used for small samples — merges into the normal as the sample size climbs. And the granddaddy of them all: by the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) , the average of many independent measurements is approximately normal no matter what distribution the raw data follows . This is why the bell curve is everywhere: nature loves averaging. 2. Transformation — “normal in disguise.” Some skewed distributions are a normal wearing a costume. If data X is lognormal (repair times, incomes, particle sizes), then ln(X) is exactly normal — take logs and the whole bell-curve toolkit comes back. Squaring and summing z-scores produces the chi-square distribution, the engine behind variance tests and goodness-of-fit tests. 3. Flexible cousins — “can imitate the normal.” The Weibull distribution, the workhorse of reliability engineering, has a shape parameter β that lets it impersonate other distributions: β = 1 makes it exactly the exponential distribution (constant failure rate), while β ≈ 3.6 makes it look strikingly like a normal. That flexibility is why Weibull is the default model for time-to-failure data. What this map does not say: it does not mean everything is secretly normal. Raw skewed data stays skewed — the CLT rescues averages , not individual values. Choosing a distribution is a modelling decision that should be driven by the data’s shape, boundaries, and physical story, and checked with plots or goodness-of-fit tests. The normal distribution as a hub: some relatives converge to it, some are transformations of it, and some can imitate it.

sections.heading: Key terminology
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Terms you’ll meet in this lesson Term Plain-language meaning Technical meaning Practical interpretation Sampling distribution The pattern you’d see if you repeated your study many times and kept the statistic each time. The probability distribution of a statistic (e.g. the sample mean) over repeated samples. It describes your average , not your raw data — the CLT is a statement about this distribution. Central Limit Theorem (CLT) Averages become bell-shaped, whatever the raw data looks like. For independent, identically distributed data with finite variance, the distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal as n grows. Justifies using z-scores and normal tables on means, even for skewed processes. Standard error (SE) The typical wobble of an average from sample to sample. SE = σ / √n, the standard deviation of the sample mean. Quadruple the sample size and the average becomes twice as precise. Weibull distribution The go-to model for “how long until it fails.” A distribution on positive values with shape β and scale η; its hazard (failure) rate rises, falls, or stays flat depending on β. β < 1: early-life failures. β = 1: random failures (exponential). β > 1: wear-out. β ≈ 3.6: nearly normal shape. Exponential distribution The waiting time for a purely random event. A Weibull with β = 1; memoryless, with a constant hazard rate. Time between random arrivals or failures — the past tells you nothing about the future. Lognormal distribution Data whose logarithm is bell-shaped. X is lognormal if ln(X) is normal with parameters μ and σ (on the log scale). Right-skewed, strictly positive data — repair times, incomes, concentrations. Log it, then use normal tools. Student’s t distribution A bell curve with fatter tails for small samples. The distribution of a standardised mean when σ is estimated from the sample; indexed by degrees of freedom (df). Use instead of the normal when n is small; by df ≈ 30 it is nearly identical to the normal. Degrees of freedom (df) How much independent information the sample carries. For a one-sample mean, df = n − 1. Low df → heavier t tails → wider intervals; high df → back to the normal. Continuity correction A half-unit adjustment when a smooth curve stands in for a staircase. Adding/subtracting 0.5 when approximating a discrete distribution (binomial, Poisson) with the continuous normal. P(X ≥ 20) for counts becomes P(X > 19.5) under the normal curve.

sections.heading: 1. The standard error of a mean (the CLT’s working part)
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
1. The standard error of a mean (the CLT’s working part)
sections.text: SE( x̄ ) = σ √ n and z = x̄ − μ σ / √ n x̄ the sample mean (average of your n measurements, in original units) μ the process (population) mean; σ the process standard deviation n the sample size (number of independent measurements averaged) SE the standard error — the standard deviation of the average , same units as the data Plain-language interpretation: averages wobble less than individual values, and the wobble shrinks with the square root of the sample size. The CLT adds the punchline: for reasonably large n (a common rule of thumb is n ≥ 30, less if the data is already symmetric), that wobble follows a normal distribution — so the z-score above works even when raw data is skewed. Assumptions: observations are independent and come from the same process with finite variance. Do not use when: data points are strongly correlated (trends, autocorrelation), the process shifts mid-sample, or n is small and the raw data is heavily skewed.

sections.text: f ( t ) = β η · ( t η ) β−1 · e −( t /η) β for t ≥ 0 t time to failure (hours, cycles, kilometres — any positive quantity) β the shape parameter (dimensionless): controls how the failure rate changes over time η the scale (characteristic life), same units as t: by this time about 63.2% of units have failed Plain-language interpretation: β is the personality, η is the size. With β = 1 the formula collapses to the exponential distribution (constant failure rate); β < 1 means failures concentrate early (infant mortality); β > 1 means failures build up with age (wear-out); and around β ≈ 3.6 the curve is so symmetric it is often mistaken for a normal. Use for: time-to-event and strength data. Not for: data that can be negative, or counts.
