sections.heading: What goes on the y-axis?
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Before we start comparing distributions on the same axes, it’s worth being precise about the vertical axis. Whenever you draw a distribution — a histogram of real data, or a smooth curve like the ones in this lesson — you have four common choices for what the height means, and they matter as soon as you try to overlay a theoretical curve on a histogram (which every tool below does). The surprising part: for a fixed dataset and bin width, all four produce the exact same shape. Changing the y-axis only relabels and rescales the height; it never bends the curve. Four ways to label the vertical axis (for a fixed dataset and bin width, the shape is identical) Y-axis Each height is… Depends on Total under it Best for Frequency the count of observations in the bin sample size and bin width area = n × bin width “how many” — raw, intuitive counts Relative frequency count ÷ n (a proportion) bin width heights sum to 1 the fraction of data in each bin Percentage 100 × count ÷ n bin width heights sum to 100 the same, expressed in % Density relative frequency ÷ bin width nothing — it’s normalised area = 1 matching theory; comparing distributions The heights are all constant multiples of each other: frequency = n · w · density, relative frequency = w · density, and percentage = 100 · w · density, where w is the bin width. Same outline, different ruler. Why density is the special one. Three properties fall out of that normalisation: Area = 1, always. Only density integrates to 1 — the defining property of a probability distribution. Every theoretical curve in this lesson (normal, Weibull, lognormal, t) is a density, so density is the only y-axis on which you can honestly lay one of those curves over a histogram. Bin-width invariance. Double your bin width and the frequency, relative-frequency, and percentage bars roughly double in height (each wider bin catches more data). Density divides that width back out, so its heights stay put — which is why the binomial checker and family explorer later work in density units. Height is not a probability. On a density axis the height is a probability per unit of x , not a probability, and it can even exceed 1 for a narrow curve. Probability is the area, never the height. This applies to the skewed distributions here too: a Weibull or lognormal histogram can be drawn on any of these axes, but you can only overlay the fitted curve in density units. Move the controls below and watch the shape hold while the axis (and the numbers on it) change. Y-axis shows Bin width: 10 Sample size n: 1000 Histogram bars Fitted normal density Method: a normal population (μ = 100, σ = 15) is split into bins of the chosen width; each bar’s expected count is n × the probability of that bin. The plot always rescales to fill the panel — that is exactly the point: the shape is fixed, only the y-axis numbers change. The dashed normal density is drawn only in density mode, because that is the one axis on which the smooth curve and the bars share a scale.

sections.heading: Two views of the same distribution: PDF and CDF
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
Two views of the same distribution: PDF and CDF
sections.text: Every distribution in this lesson — normal, Weibull, lognormal, t, exponential — comes as a matched pair. The curves you have been drawing are probability density functions , or PDFs , written f ( x ): the height is a density and the area is probability. Each one has a partner, the cumulative distribution function , or CDF , written F ( x ), which answers a running question: “what is the probability of a value at or below x ?” It climbs smoothly from 0 to 1, tracing an S-shape. (When we ask software for “the probability of failure by time t” or “the percentile of a score,” we are asking for a CDF value.) The two are tied together by the two basic operations of calculus. In plain terms: the CDF accumulates area under the PDF, and the PDF is the slope of the CDF. F ( x ) = ∫ x −∞ f ( t ) d t — integrate the PDF to accumulate the CDF f ( x ) = d F d x = F ′( x ) — differentiate the CDF to recover the PDF Read the first line as “sweep from the far left up to x , adding up density as you go — the total area so far is F ( x ).” Read the second as “how fast is that area piling up right here? That rate is the height of the PDF.” Where the bell is tall (near the mean), probability accumulates fast and the CDF climbs steeply; out in the flat tails, the CDF barely moves. Drag the point x below and watch the coupling: the shaded area in the top panel is exactly the height of the dot in the bottom panel, and the steepness of the orange tangent line in the bottom panel is exactly the height of the dot in the top panel. Drop σ below about 0.4 to see the PDF peak climb past the dashed “1.0” line — proof that a density is not a probability. Point x: 0.70 Spread σ: 1.00 density f(x) = slope of CDF 0.31 shaded area = F(x) = P(X ≤ x) 0.760 right tail P(X > x) 0.240 Method: both panels share the same horizontal axis x, with the mean μ at 0 (so at σ = 1 one unit is one standard deviation). The shaded PDF area and the CDF height are the same number, computed with the standard-normal CDF approximation; the tangent line’s slope is the PDF value f(x). Reducing σ narrows the bell and raises its peak — past σ ≈ 0.4 the peak exceeds a height of 1. The landmarks line up in a satisfying way. At the mean, the PDF is at its peak, so the CDF is at its steepest — and passes through exactly 0.5. Out in the tails, the PDF flattens toward zero, so the CDF goes nearly flat, levelling off at 0 on the left and 1 on the right. And the probability of landing between two values is an area on the PDF and a vertical gap on the CDF — the same number either way: P ( a ≤ X ≤ b ) = ∫ b a f ( x ) d x = F ( b ) − F ( a ) The integrate/differentiate link is not special to the normal — it holds for every distribution. The Weibull is a tidy example because its CDF has a clean closed form: integrating the Weibull density gives F ( t ) = 1 − e −( t /η) β This is exactly the “probability of failure by time t ” that reliability software reports. Setting t = η (the scale) gives F = 1 − e −1 ≈ 0.632 — which is why η is called the characteristic life : by that time about 63.2% of units have failed. Differentiate this CDF and you get the Weibull density back. The same idea shows up with real data too: the cumulative relative frequency curve (an ogive ) is the empirical CDF, and differencing it recovers the density histogram — the discrete mirror of differentiation.

sections.text: Don’t take the CLT on faith — watch it happen. Pick a population that is clearly not normal , choose how many measurements go into each average, and the simulator draws 2,000 sample means instantly — every slider move re-runs it. Population (raw data shape) Sample size n (values per average): 1 Histogram of 2,000 simulated sample means Normal curve predicted by the CLT Loading the first simulation… With n = 1, each “average” is just one raw value, so the histogram shows the population’s true (skewed) shape. Slide n upward and watch the bell emerge. Population mean μ Population σ Predicted SE = σ/√n Observed SD of the 2,000 means Method: for each of 2,000 repetitions, the simulator draws n random values from the chosen population and records their average. The dashed overlay is a normal curve with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n, scaled to the histogram’s area. Randomness means your histogram will look slightly different each run — that is the point. Notice two things: the bell appears and it gets narrower — the √n in the standard error at work. Then try the bimodal population: even two separate peaks can’t resist averaging.

sections.heading: Step-by-step: choosing the right distribution
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Identify the data type. Continuous measurement, time-to-event, count of events, or count of successes out of n trials? This alone eliminates most wrong choices. Plot the data. Histogram plus, ideally, a probability plot. Note symmetry versus skew, boundaries (can it be negative? is it capped?), and the number of peaks. Match the physical story. Sum of many small effects → normal. Product of many small effects → lognormal. Time until a random event → exponential. Time until wear-out → Weibull with β > 1. Successes in n trials → binomial. Rare-event counts → Poisson. Check whether you’re analysing raw values or averages. If your question is about a mean and n is reasonably large, the CLT usually lets you use normal methods regardless of step 3 (with SE = σ/√n; use Student’s t when σ is estimated from a small sample). Fit and verify. Estimate parameters in software, then check the fit with a probability plot or goodness-of-fit statistic (e.g. Anderson–Darling: lower is better, and its p-value should not be small). Apply the model. Compute the probabilities, percentiles, or reliability figures the question asks for — using continuity correction if a normal is standing in for a discrete distribution. Document. Record the chosen distribution, fitted parameters, sample size, fit evidence, and any transformations (especially logs), so the analysis can be audited and repeated.

sections.heading: Worked example: skewed data, normal answer
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
Worked example: skewed data, normal answer
sections.text: The problem: a support centre’s individual call-handling times are strongly right-skewed (a lognormal-ish shape): most calls are quick, a few drag on. Management asks: “On a day when we handle 36 calls, what is the chance the day’s average handling time exceeds 10 minutes?” The data: long-run records show the population of individual call times has mean μ = 8 minutes and standard deviation σ = 6 minutes. Calls can be treated as independent. The method: the question is about an average of n = 36 values. Even though raw call times are skewed, the CLT says the sample mean is approximately normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n. So: compute the standard error, standardise, and read off the tail. The formula: z = x̄ − μ σ / √ n Substitute the values: z = 10 − 8 6 / √ 36 Intermediate calculations: √36 = 6 , so the standard error is SE = 6 ÷ 6 = 1 minute . (Individual calls wobble by 6 minutes; a 36-call average wobbles by only 1.) The numerator is 10 − 8 = 2 minutes . z = 2 ÷ 1 = 2.0 . Final answer: a 10-minute daily average sits 2 standard errors above the expected average. From the 68–95–99.7 rule (or software), the probability beyond +2 is about 2.3% . Practical interpretation: only about 1 day in 44 should see an average above 10 minutes by chance alone. If it happens repeatedly, something about the process has genuinely changed — staffing, call mix, or system issues — and it’s worth investigating rather than blaming luck. Limitations: the CLT approximation is good here because n = 36 is respectable, but with heavily skewed data and small n (say, 5 calls) it would be unsafe. We also used the long-run σ as if known; if σ were estimated from a small sample, Student’s t (df = n − 1) would be the honest choice.

sections.heading: Interpretation guide
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: When you see this, it means this When you see… It means… Raw data skewed, but histogram of daily averages looks bell-shaped The CLT at work — normal methods are fine for the averages, not for individual values. A fitted Weibull with β < 1 Failure rate is decreasing : early-life (infant-mortality) failures dominate. Suspect manufacturing or installation defects; burn-in testing may help. A fitted Weibull with β ≈ 1 Roughly constant failure rate — effectively exponential; failures are random and age-independent. Preventive replacement won’t help much. A fitted Weibull with β > 1 (say 2–5) Failure rate increases with age: wear-out. Scheduled maintenance or replacement makes sense. Right-skewed positive data whose histogram of ln(x) looks normal Lognormal behaviour — analyse on the log scale, then transform conclusions back. A t-distribution curve noticeably wider than the normal Small sample: extra uncertainty from estimating σ. Expect wider confidence intervals. np or n(1−p) below about 10 The binomial is skewed — don’t substitute a normal curve; use exact binomial calculations. An Anderson–Darling p-value below 0.05 on a normality test Evidence the data is not normal — consider a relative (lognormal, Weibull) or a transformation.

sections.heading: 1. Applying the CLT to a single value Interpretation error
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
1. Applying the CLT to a single value Interpretation error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: the CLT normalises averages , not raw observations. One call, one part, one invoice still follows the skewed population distribution. How to recognise it: a “probability” for an individual value computed with σ/√n. How to avoid it: ask first: is the question about one value (use σ) or an average (use σ/√n)?

sections.heading: 2. Forgetting the √n in the standard error Calculation error
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
2. Forgetting the √n in the standard error Calculation error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: using σ/n makes averages look far too precise; using plain σ makes them look far too noisy. How to recognise it: z-scores that are wildly large or suspiciously tiny for a mean. How to avoid it: memorise the sanity check — quadrupling n should halve the SE, not quarter it.

sections.heading: 3. Swapping Weibull shape and scale Software-output error
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
3. Swapping Weibull shape and scale Software-output error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: β (shape) and η (scale) play completely different roles; Excel’s WEIBULL.DIST(x, alpha, beta, ...) uses alpha for shape and beta for scale — the Greek letters don’t match the common engineering notation, and it trips people constantly. How to recognise it: a fitted “shape” of 5,000 hours, or a characteristic life of 2.3. How to avoid it: the shape parameter is dimensionless and usually between 0.3 and 6; the scale carries the time units.

breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
4. Exponentiating a log-scale mean and calling it “the mean” Interpretation error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: for lognormal data, e mean of ln(x) is the median of x, not the mean — the true mean is higher (e μ+σ²/2 ). How to recognise it: a “mean repair time” that sits suspiciously below most textbook summaries of the same data. How to avoid it: decide up front whether the median (typical case) or mean (total-workload planning) answers the business question — for skewed data they genuinely differ.

5. Using the normal approximation with small np Assumption error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: when np < 10 (or n(1−p) < 10) the binomial is skewed and pressed against a boundary, so symmetric-normal tail probabilities can be badly wrong. How to recognise it: approximate answers that differ wildly from exact BINOM.DIST results, or negative “possible” counts. How to avoid it: check np and n(1−p) before approximating — the interactive checker above shows exactly why.

6. Skipping the continuity correction Exam trap
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: a smooth curve is standing in for whole-number bars, so P(X ≥ 20) corresponds to the area beyond 19.5, not 20. How to recognise it: your answer differs from the marking scheme by a consistent small margin. How to avoid it: when approximating binomial or Poisson counts with a normal, widen the region by 0.5 in the direction that includes the boundary value.

7. Reaching for t only when data “looks weird” Assumption error
sections.text: Why it’s wrong: Student’s t is not a fix for non-normal data — it corrects for estimating σ from a small sample of (roughly) normal data. How to recognise it: a t-test quoted on 8 wildly skewed observations as if the t fixed the skew. How to avoid it: small n + estimated σ → t; skewed data → transformation, a better-fitting distribution, or a nonparametric method.

sections.text: Where to find it: Graph › Probability Distribution Plot draws and shades any of these distributions. To identify which relative fits your data best, use Stat › Quality Tools › Individual Distribution Identification — it fits normal, lognormal, Weibull, exponential and more, side by side. Output that matters: for each candidate distribution, look at the probability plot (points near the line = good fit) and the Anderson–Darling (AD) statistic — smaller is better, and a p-value above 0.05 means no evidence against that distribution. For reliability work, Stat › Reliability/Survival › Distribution Analysis reports the Weibull shape and scale with confidence intervals. Common Minitab mistake: picking the distribution with the prettiest curve instead of comparing AD statistics, and ignoring that several distributions may fit almost equally well — when they do, prefer the one with the stronger physical justification.

sections.heading: Practice activity: the maintenance manager’s week
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
Practice activity: the maintenance manager’s week
sections.text: Scenario: you’re reviewing two datasets for a plant maintenance manager. Pump bearings: a Weibull analysis of time-to-failure data returns shape β = 0.7 and scale η = 18,000 hours. The manager plans to introduce scheduled replacement of old bearings at 12,000 hours. Is that plan well-aimed? Repair times: individual repair jobs are right-skewed with population mean μ = 5 hours and standard deviation σ = 4 hours . Next month the team will complete n = 64 jobs. Estimate the probability that the month’s average repair time exceeds 6 hours . Work through both (the interpretation guide and the SE formula are all you need), then check yourself. 1. The plan is aimed at the wrong problem. A shape parameter of β = 0.7 is below 1 , which means a decreasing failure rate: bearings that survive their early life become more reliable, not less. Failures are concentrated in infancy — likely installation or manufacturing defects. Replacing old (surviving) bearings at 12,000 hours would discard the most reliable units and install new ones that carry fresh infant-mortality risk. Better actions: improve installation practices, incoming inspection, or burn-in — and investigate the early failures. Scheduled age-based replacement only makes sense for wear-out behaviour (β > 1). 2. About 2.3%. The question concerns an average of n = 64 jobs, so the CLT applies despite the skew: SE = σ / √n = 4 / √64 = 4 / 8 = 0.5 hours . z = (x̄ − μ) / SE = (6 − 5) / 0.5 = +2.0 . The area beyond +2 on a normal curve is about 2.3% (from the 68–95–99.7 rule: (100% − 95%) ÷ 2). The reasoning pattern: question about an average → standard error with √n → z-score → empirical rule. Note the contrast with part 1: there, the question was about individual lifetimes , so the CLT was irrelevant and the Weibull shape parameter carried the answer.

sections.heading: Key takeaways
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: The normal distribution is the hub of a family: some distributions converge to it, some are transformations of it, and some can imitate it. The Central Limit Theorem makes averages approximately normal regardless of the raw data’s shape — with spread SE = σ/√n. Precision grows with √n: four times the data buys twice the precision of the mean. Weibull’s shape parameter tells the failure story: β < 1 infant mortality, β = 1 random (exponential), β > 1 wear-out, β ≈ 3.6 near-normal. Lognormal data is a normal in disguise: take logs, use the bell-curve toolkit, and remember e μ is the median . Student’s t is the normal’s small-sample stand-in — heavier tails that fade as df grows; it corrects for estimating σ, not for skew. Approximate a binomial with a normal only when np and n(1−p) are both at least about 10, and use a continuity correction. Choose distributions by data type, shape, boundaries, and the physical story — then verify with a probability plot or Anderson–Darling test.

sections.heading: Decision rule
breadcrumb: Beyond the Bell: The Normal Distribution and Its Relatives
sections.text: Question about an average with decent n → CLT: use the normal with SE = σ/√n (or t if σ is estimated from a small sample). Question about individual values → model the raw data: symmetric → normal; positive and right-skewed → lognormal or Weibull; time-to-failure → Weibull (read β); success counts → binomial (approximate with a normal only if np and n(1−p) ≥ 10). Remember this: the CLT rescues averages, not individuals — and √n is doing the heavy lifting. Suggested next lesson: revisit The Normal Distribution: Meet the Bell Curve if any foundations felt shaky, or continue to Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing Basics , where the standard error and Student’s t from this lesson become your everyday tools.

sections.heading: Exact Minitab workflow: polynomial regression with validated selection
breadcrumb: Finding the Best Predictive Regression Model in Minitab
Exact Minitab workflow: polynomial regression with validated selection
sections.text: The sequence below is designed for a continuous response and a mix of continuous and categorical predictors. 1 Define the model purpose and data boundary Prediction target, operating range, grouping unit, and holdout logic ⌄ State what the model will predict, for which population, and within what process range. Decide whether the validation target is a new row, a new heat, a new coil, a future campaign, or a later time period. Exclude post-outcome variables and data created after the prediction decision. Flag impossible values, missingness, duplicate records, and data-quality rules before fitting. Reserve a true future or external test set when the decision is high consequence. 2 Open Fit Regression Model Assign the response and predictor types correctly ⌄ Stat → Regression → Regression → Fit Regression Model Enter the continuous outcome in Response . Enter numeric process inputs in Continuous predictors . Enter grade, mill, product family, shift, operator, or other factors in Categorical predictors . Verify the categorical reference level under Coding so coefficients compare against a meaningful baseline. 3 Create the candidate term pool Main effects, squares, and two-way interactions ⌄ Fit Regression Model → Model Select the continuous predictors you want to expand. Choose Terms through order . Enter 2 . Click Add . Review the term list and remove combinations that are physically impossible, redundant, or unsupported. Terms through order 2 adds individual squares for continuous predictors and all interactions through order 2 among the selected predictors. 4 Center continuous predictors Reduce nonessential collinearity from powers and interactions ⌄ Fit Regression Model → Coding → Standardize continuous predictors → Subtract the mean Centering changes each predictor from X to X − X̄. This reduces the artificial correlation between X, X², and interaction terms and makes lower-order coefficients meaningful near the center of the observed operating region. X centered = X − X̄ Do not confuse centering with dividing by the standard deviation. Scaling can be useful for coefficient comparison, but it changes the unit interpretation. 5 Configure forward selection with validation Let validation choose the model size ⌄ Fit Regression Model → Stepwise Method: Forward selection with validation Validation: K-fold cross-validation for smaller data; test-set validation for larger data Folds: 5 or 10 are practical starting points; Minitab’s regression default is 10 Group-aware folds: Assign rows by a prepared fold-ID column Display: Include model-selection details Graph: Display R² versus model-selection step How it works: within each fold, Minitab performs forward selection. It then evaluates the sequence across folds and identifies the step with the best K-fold stepwise R². Finally, it runs forward selection on the full dataset and stops at that selected step. 6 Enforce hierarchy Keep higher-order terms statistically coherent ⌄ Stepwise → Hierarchy Hierarchical model: Require a hierarchical model at each step Require hierarchy for: All terms Terms entering: Extra terms can enter to maintain hierarchy For X₁X₂, retain X₁ and X₂. For X₁³, retain X₁ and X₁². For X₁²X₂, retain the applicable lower-order components required by the hierarchy rule. 7 Request diagnostics and stored statistics Do not stop at the selected equation ⌄ Fit Regression Model → Graphs / Results / Storage Display the four-in-one residual plots. Display VIF values and unusual observations. Store fits, residuals, standardized residuals, leverage, Cook’s distance, and DFITS when deeper investigation is needed. Plot residuals against production order or timestamp when the process is time-dependent. 8 Interpret the validation curve—not only the peak Prefer a stable plateau over a fragile maximum ⌄ If the highest validation R² occurs at step 12 but steps 7–10 are nearly identical, prefer the simpler model unless the additional terms provide a material, repeatable improvement. Compare training R² with validation R². Look for a widening training–validation gap. Check whether selected terms are stable under alternate fold assignments. Confirm coefficient directions and interactions make engineering sense. Stepwise selection is exploratory. It cannot incorporate every practical consideration, can choose one of several correlated predictors arbitrarily, and can produce different “best” models under different criteria. Treat selected-term p-values cautiously and validate with new data whenever possible. Step 4

sections.heading: A defensible model-selection rule
breadcrumb: Finding the Best Predictive Regression Model in Minitab
sections.text: Do not allow a single metric to decide. Use sequential gates so that a model cannot “win” on accuracy while failing interpretability, stability, or process logic. Gate 1: Valid design No leakage, correct grouping, correct prediction horizon, and no post-outcome predictors. Gate 2: Competitive error Validation error meets the practical tolerance and is close to the best challenger. Gate 3: Adequate diagnostics No unresolved structural residual pattern, severe instability, or dominant data defect. Gate 4: Engineering utility Interpretation, measurement burden, deployment feasibility, and safe operating range are acceptable. Recommended final decision statement: “MARS was selected because its grouped five-fold validation RMSE was within 3% of the best model, while providing substantially greater interpretability and stable predictor effects. The model passed residual, influence, and operating-range checks. TreeNet was retained as a benchmark but not selected for deployment.”

sections.heading: 5. Variable-selection methods in the Stepwise dialog
breadcrumb: 5. Variable-selection methods in the Stepwise dialog
sections.text: The methods in Minitab’s Stepwise dialog differ in three fundamental ways: where the search starts, whether terms can enter or leave, and what rule controls the next move. The examples below use six candidate predictors—A, B, C, D, E, and F—so you can see exactly how each method proceeds. Method Starts with Can enter? Can leave? Main selection rule Typical use None User-defined model No No No automatic selection Predefined engineering model Stepwise Usually intercept or initial terms Yes Yes Entry and removal p-values Flexible screening Forward Selection Small model Yes No Smallest qualifying p-value Simple sequential selection Backward Elimination Full model No Yes Largest nonqualifying p-value removed Reduce a plausible full model Forward Information Criteria Small model Yes Typically no AIC/AICc-type improvement Fit-complexity balance Forward Selection with Validation Small model Yes No along forward path Stepwise rule builds path; validation selects step Prediction-focused model-size selection Common setup for the examples: assume the candidate predictors are A, B, C, D, E, and F. For p-value-based methods, suppose the alpha-to-enter and alpha-to-remove thresholds are both 0.15 unless stated otherwise. 5.1 None — fit exactly the model you specify With None , Minitab performs no variable-selection search. You decide the model before fitting it. If you place A, B, C, and the interaction A×B in the model, Minitab fits exactly that equation: Y = β₀ + β₁A + β₂B + β₃C + β₄(A×B) Minitab does not ask whether D, E, or F should enter, and it does not remove A, B, C, or A×B automatically.

sections.heading: 7.9 The hierarchy principle
sections.text: Best Subsets treats an interaction column as an ordinary numeric predictor. It does not automatically understand that A_B represents A×B or that A and B should accompany it. This means Best Subsets can return a mathematically possible but structurally undesirable model such as: Y = β₀ + β₁(A×B) In most engineering and statistical applications, prefer the hierarchical form: Y = β₀ + β₁A + β₂B + β₃(A×B) This is called the principle of hierarchy . When an interaction is retained, the associated lower-order main effects should ordinarily remain in the model.
sections.excerpt: Best Subsets treats an interaction column as an ordinary numeric predictor. It does not automatically understand that A_B represents A×B or that A and B should accompany it. This means Best Subsets can return a mathematically possible but structurally…

sections.heading: Why hierarchy matters
sections.text: The interaction describes how the effect of A changes with B. Without A and B, the coefficient of A×B becomes difficult to interpret. Dropping the main effects can make the result depend strongly on how the variables are centered or coded. Hierarchical models are usually easier to communicate and defend scientifically.

sections.heading: Example interpretation
sections.text: For the hierarchical model: Y = β₀ + β₁A + β₂B + β₃(A×B) The effect of A is not just β₁. It depends on B: Effect of A = β₁ + β₃B Similarly, the effect of B depends on A: Effect of B = β₂ + β₃A Because the main effects are conditional when an interaction is present, interpret them at meaningful reference values. Centering continuous predictors before creating interaction columns often makes the coefficients easier to interpret.

sections.heading: 7.11 Recommended Best Subsets workflow with interactions
breadcrumb: 7.11 Recommended Best Subsets workflow with interactions
sections.text: Use engineering knowledge, prior studies, process maps, or DOE principles to identify plausible interactions and curved terms. Create those interaction and polynomial columns using Calc → Calculator . Run Best Subsets using the main effects and the manually created derived terms. Review the strongest candidate models, but reject nonhierarchical combinations unless there is a compelling technical reason. Rebuild the chosen candidate in Fit Regression Model . Check hierarchy, VIF, residual plots, influential observations, predicted R², and engineering plausibility. Validate the final model on new or held-out data before using it for decisions or prediction. Best practice: use Best Subsets to generate candidate models, then finalize the model in Fit Regression Model, where you can explicitly control main effects, interactions, polynomial terms, hierarchy, diagnostics, and interpretation.

Place the continuous predictors in Continuous predictors . For example, use Carbon, Rolling Temperature, Cooling Rate, and Thickness. Place categorical predictors, such as grade, rolling practice, production line, or furnace, in the appropriate categorical or factor field. Do not manually multiply text-coded categories to create interaction columns. Click Model... . Highlight the predictors that should participate in the interaction structure. Choose Interactions through order 2 to generate all two-way interactions among the selected predictors. Click Add . Minitab adds the requested main effects and interaction terms to the model specification. Return to the main dialog and click Stepwise... if automatic term selection is required. Choose Stepwise, Forward Selection, Backward Elimination, Forward Information Criteria, or Forward Selection with Validation, depending on your modeling purpose. Use the hierarchy controls so lower-order terms remain whenever a higher-order interaction or polynomial term is retained.

Which model size predicts new data best? Forward Selection with Validation Uses validation to choose among models along the forward path. Is a curved polynomial relationship adequate? Fitted Line Plot or Fit Regression Model Polynomial regression is still linear in coefficients. What are the parameters in a known nonlinear equation? Nonlinear Regression Uses iterative estimation for nonlinear parameters. Is the response yes/no? Binary Logistic Regression Models probability rather than an unbounded continuous response. sections.heading: 10.1 R²
sections.text: R² measures the percentage of observed response variation explained by the fitted model. It never decreases when predictors are added, so it can reward unnecessary complexity.

sections.heading: 10.2 Adjusted R²
sections.text: Adjusted R² penalizes the addition of terms that do not improve the model enough. It is more useful than R² for comparing models with different numbers of predictors.

sections.heading: 10.3 Predicted R²
sections.text: Predicted R² estimates how well the model predicts observations that were not used to estimate the coefficients. A large gap between adjusted R² and predicted R² can indicate overfitting, influential observations, or instability.

sections.heading: 10.4 Mallows’ Cp

sections.heading: 10.6 P-values
sections.text: A coefficient p-value tests whether the data provide evidence that the adjusted coefficient differs from zero, given the other terms in the current model. It does not establish causality, practical importance, or predictive value by itself.

sections.heading: 10.7 VIF
sections.text: Variance Inflation Factors diagnose multicollinearity. Large VIF values mean that a coefficient is being estimated with greater uncertainty because predictors overlap in the information they provide.

sections.heading: 11. Recommended practical workflow
sections.text: Define the response and purpose. Is the goal explanation, prediction, optimization, or screening? Confirm the response type. Continuous, binary, ordinal, nominal, or count? Plot the data. Use scatterplots, matrix plots, time plots, and fitted line plots. Use engineering knowledge. Identify required terms, likely interactions, physical bounds, and confounders. Fit a reasonable full model. Review coefficient signs, p-values, VIF, residual plots, leverage, and influential points. Use selection methods as screening tools. Compare Forward, Stepwise, Backward, and Best Subsets rather than blindly trusting one method. Validate. Use validation data, predicted R², PRESS-type results, or cross-validation where available. Choose the simplest defensible model. Prefer a model that is stable, interpretable, and nearly as predictive as larger alternatives. Confirm assumptions. Linearity, constant variance, residual normality where relevant, independence, and absence of severe influence. Document the final equation and its limits. State the data range, intended use, uncertainty, and conditions under which predictions are valid.

sections.text: Download the practice dataset below and work through the exercises in Minitab. It is a fictitious steel-coil dataset with 50 rows and 10 columns : an identifier, one response (Tensile Strength), and eight candidate predictors. It was built on purpose to contain useful predictors, one mostly irrelevant predictor, mild collinearity, a Carbon × Cooling Rate interaction, Rolling Temperature curvature, and random noise — so every selection method has something to reveal. ⇩ Download the practice dataset (Excel .xlsx) Column Role What it does in the data Coil ID Identifier Row label only — not a predictor. Tensile Strength (MPa) Response (Y) The variable you model and predict. Carbon (wt%) Predictor Strong, useful predictor. Manganese (wt%) Predictor Useful, but mildly collinear with Carbon. Rolling Temperature (°C) Predictor Curved (quadratic) effect; strength peaks mid-range. Cooling Rate (°C/s) Predictor Useful; interacts with Carbon. Thickness (mm) Predictor Useful; more thickness lowers strength. Furnace Time (min) Predictor Weak-to-moderate; mildly collinear with Rolling Temperature. Line Speed (m/min) Predictor Very weak effect. Ambient Humidity (%) Predictor Mostly irrelevant noise — a good test for selection methods. Before you start. The workbook has two tabs: Practice Data (load this into Minitab) and Data Dictionary (documents every column and the structure built into the data). When you choose predictors, ignore Coil ID — it is only a row label.

sections.heading: 14. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
breadcrumb: 14. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
sections.text: Mistake 1: Treating variable selection as proof Automatic selection is exploratory. It does not prove that selected terms are causal or that omitted variables are unimportant. Mistake 2: Believing forward selection searches every model Forward selection follows one path. Best Subsets is the more exhaustive procedure for moderate predictor counts. Mistake 3: Believing validation chooses the next variable in Minitab’s forward-validation method The forward stepwise rule determines the sequence. Validation chooses the preferred model size along that sequence. Mistake 4: Choosing the largest R² R² always favors larger models. Compare adjusted R², predicted R², S, C p , validation error, and practical simplicity. Mistake 5: Calling every curve “nonlinear regression” A polynomial curve is still linear regression if the unknown coefficients enter linearly. Mistake 6: Ignoring hierarchy If an interaction or squared term is included, retain the associated lower-order terms unless there is a strong, defensible reason not to. Mistake 7: Ignoring residual diagnostics A selected model can still violate assumptions, contain influential points, or show unmodeled curvature. Mistake 8: Extrapolating beyond the data Regression predictions outside the observed predictor range can be physically unrealistic and highly uncertain.

sections.heading: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
breadcrumb: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
sections.text: Once you have chosen a model, a common next step is to predict the response at particular predictor values — for example, “what tensile strength should I expect at these settings?” You could substitute the values into the fitted equation by hand, but the reliable approach is to let Minitab predict from the stored model , because it also reports the uncertainty around the prediction. This section shows the official workflow, a worked example, and how to read the output.

sections.heading: 15.1 First make sure the model is stored
breadcrumb: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
15.1 First make sure the model is stored
sections.text: Best Subsets Regression only identifies candidate models — it does not leave behind a fitted model that Minitab can predict from. So if you are working from Best Subsets, refit your chosen subset with Fit Regression Model first. Stat → Regression → Regression → Fit Regression Model In the Best Subsets output, identify the model you selected using the X marks in its row. Enter your response (Y). Enter the selected predictors as continuous or categorical terms. Under Model , add the exact interaction and polynomial terms that the chosen subset includes. Check the residual plots and model assumptions, then click OK . This creates a stored regression model . Everything in the Predict step below uses that stored equation, so the model must exist before you can predict from it.

Click Options and normally keep Confidence level 95% and Interval type: Two-sided . Click OK . Minitab uses the stored equation to calculate the prediction. To predict at many settings at once, choose Enter columns of values instead and point Minitab at worksheet columns holding the predictor settings — it returns one prediction per row.

sections.heading: 15.3 Worked example
breadcrumb: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
sections.text: Suppose your fitted equation is: ŷ = 10 + 2A − 1.5B + 0.4(A × B) and you want the predicted response at A = 3 and B = 4 . Minitab computes: ŷ = 10 + 2(3) − 1.5(4) + 0.4(3 × 4) = 10 + 6 − 6 + 4.8 = 14.8 So the predicted response is ŷ = 14.8 . Entering interaction terms correctly. If A×B was added through the Model dialog, enter only A = 3 and B = 4 — Minitab computes the interaction for you. If instead you built an A_B worksheet column manually before running Best Subsets, Minitab will ask for that column too, and you must enter its value yourself: Predictor Value to enter A 3 B 4 A_B 3 × 4 = 12

sections.heading: 15.4 Understanding the prediction output
breadcrumb: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
sections.text: Output What it means Fit The best point estimate of the response at those settings. SE Fit The uncertainty in that estimated mean response. 95% CI A range for the average response at those settings. 95% PI A range for a single individual future result at those settings. For our example the output might read: Fit 95% CI 95% PI 14.8 13.9 – 15.7 11.2 – 18.4 Read that as: The estimated average response at these settings is 14.8 . That average is likely between 13.9 and 15.7 (the 95% confidence interval). One new result could reasonably fall between 11.2 and 18.4 (the 95% prediction interval). Confidence interval vs. prediction interval. When you care about a single future coil, heat, slab, or test result, the prediction interval is the one that matters. It is wider than the confidence interval because an individual outcome carries more variation than an estimated average.

sections.heading: 15.5 A caution on extrapolation
breadcrumb: 15. Predicting a response at specific predictor settings
sections.text: Avoid predicting far outside the predictor ranges used to build the model. Minitab may flag such settings as unusual (an X in the output), and extrapolated predictions can be unreliable because the fitted relationship was never verified in that region. Exam tip (CSSBB/CQE). Be ready to distinguish the confidence interval for the mean response from the prediction interval for an individual value, and to pick the prediction interval when a question asks about one future outcome. Knowing the Predict menu path and that interactions/polynomials must be present in the stored model is frequently tested in applied items.

sections.heading: 16. Final summary
sections.text: Method Best concise description Fitted Line Plot Visual simple regression for one continuous X and one continuous Y. Fit Regression Model — None Fits exactly the linear model you specify. Forward Selection Adds qualifying predictors one at a time and usually does not remove them. Backward Elimination Starts full and removes weak terms. Stepwise Allows predictors to enter and leave according to significance rules. Forward Information Criteria Adds predictors according to a fit-versus-complexity criterion. Forward Selection with Validation Builds one forward path, then uses validation to select the preferred step. Best Subsets Compares many or all predictor combinations and presents leading models by size. Nonlinear Regression Fits a user-specified scientific equation that is nonlinear in its parameters. Best overall principle: use selection procedures to generate candidate models, not to replace engineering judgment. The final model should be statistically sound, physically credible, interpretable, stable, validated, and appropriate for the intended decision.

sections.heading: Control charts in plain English
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: A control chart is a time-ordered process graph with statistically calculated limits. It answers: “Is the process behaving like one stable system, or is something unusual changing it?”
sections.excerpt: A control chart is a time-ordered process graph with statistically calculated limits. It answers: “Is the process behaving like one stable system, or is something unusual changing it?”

sections.heading: What a control chart tells you

What a control chart tells you
sections.text: Whether variation appears consistent over time. Whether an unusual point, shift, trend, cycle, or mixture pattern may require investigation. Whether process changes produced a sustained change.

breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart

sections.heading: Key terminology
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Term Plain-language meaning Practical interpretation Common-cause variation Routine background variation built into the current system. Improve the system; do not chase individual points. Special-cause variation An unusual source that is not consistently present. Investigate the specific time, material, setup, equipment, operator, or environment. Center line The expected process level or rate. Usually estimated from baseline data unless a validated historical parameter is entered. Control limits Expected boundaries for a stable process. Usually based on approximately ±3 standard deviations, with chart-specific distributions. Specification limits Engineering or customer acceptance requirements. They evaluate conformance, not stability. They should not replace control limits. Rational subgroup Observations collected under nearly identical short-term conditions. Within-subgroup variation represents short-term noise; between-subgroup differences reveal process changes. Defective A unit classified once as pass/fail. Use P, NP, or Laney P′ charts. Defect An individual nonconformity; one unit may have several. Use C, U, or Laney U′ charts. Phase I Establish and clean a historical baseline. Investigate special causes and estimate defensible limits. Phase II Monitor future production against established limits. Use frozen historical limits unless the process is intentionally changed.

sections.heading: Xbar-R
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Best for: monitoring the subgroup mean and within-subgroup range when subgroup size is generally 2–8. Stat > Control Charts > Variables Charts for Subgroups > Xbar-R Example: five thickness readings every hour. Read the R chart first, then the Xbar chart. Use time-ordered rational subgroups. Step-by-step Minitab setup Place measurements in one column with a subgroup ID column, or place each subgroup across one row. Open the menu path above. Select the appropriate data arrangement. Enter the measurement column(s) and subgroup IDs or subgroup size. Select Xbar-R Options > Tests to add company-approved special-cause tests. Select OK . Evaluate R before Xbar. Use another chart when Use Xbar-S for subgroup sizes of 9 or more. Use I-MR-R/S when each subgroup is a distinct batch or part with a consistent within-item variation source.
sections.excerpt: Best for: monitoring the subgroup mean and within-subgroup range when subgroup size is generally 2–8. Stat > Control Charts > Variables Charts for Subgroups > Xbar-R Example: five thickness readings every hour. Read the R chart first, then the Xbar chart. Use…

sections.heading: Xbar-S
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Best for: monitoring mean and standard deviation with larger subgroups, generally 9 or more. Stat > Control Charts > Variables Charts for Subgroups > Xbar-S Example: 12 hardness readings per plate. S uses every observation and is more efficient than range for larger subgroups. Read S first, then Xbar. Step-by-step Minitab setup Arrange the subgroup observations in columns plus subgroup ID, or across rows. Open Xbar-S. Specify variables and subgroup structure. Use Xbar-S Options for tests, stages, and historical parameters. Create the chart and investigate S-chart signals before mean signals. Use another chart when Use Xbar-R for smaller subgroups. Use I-MR-R/S for repeated measurements within distinct batches or parts.

sections.heading: I-MR-R/S (Between/Within)
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Best for: separating variation within each distinct part or batch from variation between consecutive parts or batches. Stat > Control Charts > Variables Charts for Subgroups > I-MR-R/S (Between/Within) Produces three panels: I, MR, and either R or S. R/S measures within-subgroup variation. MR measures between-subgroup variation using consecutive subgroup means. Step-by-step Minitab setup Ensure each subgroup represents a distinct batch, part, coil, or repeated-measure unit. Arrange one row per subgroup or use one measurement column plus subgroup IDs. Open the path above and enter the data structure. Use I-MR-R/S Options for tests, stages, and known parameters. Interpret R/S first, MR second, I last. Steel example Five gauge readings across each coil: R/S assesses within-coil uniformity, MR assesses coil-to-coil changes in average gauge, and I assesses the sequence of coil means.

breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Best for: monitoring subgroup means only when dispersion is already being evaluated separately. Stat > Control Charts > Variables Charts for Subgroups > Xbar Step-by-step Minitab setup Enter subgroup measurements and IDs. Open Xbar. Specify the variables and subgroup structure. Use Xbar Options for tests or historical parameters. Do not interpret the chart unless short-term variation is stable. For routine work, Xbar-R or Xbar-S is usually safer because it displays the companion variation chart.

Create the chart and investigate sudden increases, decreases, trends, or nonrandom patterns in range. R compares values inside the same subgroup. It is not the same as MR, which compares consecutive time points.

sections.text: Best for: monitoring individual continuous values and their short-term moving ranges. Step-by-step Minitab setup Place the measurement in one column, sorted chronologically. Open I-MR. Enter the variable column. sections.text: Best for: short-run monitoring across products, sizes, grades, or targets with different means and standard deviations. Confirm that product-specific reference values are defensible before interpreting signals. Do not mix unlike products on a conventional I-MR chart without standardization.

sections.heading: Time-Weighted Charts
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Continuous data where small sustained shifts matter These charts use information from previous observations. They can detect small persistent shifts earlier than traditional Shewhart charts when designed and interpreted correctly.

sections.heading: CUSUM
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Best for: detecting a small persistent shift from a defined target by accumulating deviations. Stat > Control Charts > Time-Weighted Charts > CUSUM Step-by-step Minitab setup Use individual observations or subgroup means in time order. Define the target mean and an appropriate standard deviation. Open CUSUM and enter the variable plus subgroup information if applicable. Specify the shift size or CUSUM parameters based on the operationally meaningful change. Interpret upper and lower cumulative paths against decision boundaries. CUSUM does not use Minitab’s standard tests-for-special-causes menu.

sections.text: Best for: detecting small sustained mean shifts while weighting recent observations more heavily. Stat > Control Charts > Time-Weighted Charts > EWMA Step-by-step Minitab setup Prepare chronological individual values or subgroup means. Open EWMA and enter the variable plus subgroup information if used. Enter the EWMA weight λ; smaller values create stronger smoothing. Use a validated target and standard deviation where available. Investigate points beyond EWMA limits or sustained movement toward a limit.

sections.heading: Minitab special-cause tests

sections.text: Test Pattern What it can suggest 1 One point more than 3σ from the center line A large isolated special cause. 2 Nine points in a row on the same side A sustained process shift. 3 Six points in a row increasing or decreasing A trend or drift. 4 Fourteen points alternating up and down Systematic over-adjustment or alternating sources. 5 Two of three points more than 2σ from the center line on the same side A moderate shift. 6 Four of five points more than 1σ from the center line on the same side A small sustained shift. 7 Fifteen points in a row within 1σ of the center line Stratification or control limits that are too wide. 8 Eight points in a row more than 1σ from the center line on either side A mixture pattern or limits that are too narrow for the data structure. Availability varies by chart. Minitab provides Tests 1–8 for most variables charts; R, S, MR, and attribute charts support fewer tests; EWMA and Moving Average support only Test 1; CUSUM, Zone, and multivariate charts use their own signaling logic.

sections.heading: Interpretation guide: when you see this, it means this
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
Interpretation guide: when you see this, it means this
sections.text: When you see this What it may mean What to do next Variation chart out of control The short-term variation estimate is unstable. Investigate variation signals first; delay conclusions from the mean chart. One point beyond a control limit A large special cause may have occurred. Trace the exact time to material, equipment, setup, measurement, and operating records. Nine points on one side The process level may have shifted. Identify a change point, verify whether it was intentional, and consider staged limits. Six points steadily increasing A drift may be occurring. Check wear, thermal buildup, tool condition, calibration drift, or progressive material change. P or U limits change each subgroup Sample size or opportunity varies. Do not force constant limits; verify the subgroup-size column is correct. Many P/U signals with huge samples Overdispersion, underdispersion, or mixed process structure may exist. Investigate the structure, then assess Laney P′ or U′ if appropriate. G/T point becomes very low Rare adverse events are occurring closer together. Escalate the investigation even though low values may look visually “better” on ordinary charts. T² signal with stable univariate charts The joint combination of variables is unusual. Examine contributions, correlations, and process context rather than dismissing the signal. All points inside limits but process misses specs The process may be stable but incapable. Perform capability analysis after confirming stability.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and software traps
breadcrumb: Minitab Control Charts: Select, Build, and Interpret the Right Chart
sections.text: Selection error: using P for defects. A P chart counts defective units, not multiple defects. Use C/U/Laney U′ for defects. Subgroup error: grouping unrelated observations. A subgroup should represent short-term common conditions, not a convenient set of five rows. Interpretation error: reading Xbar before R or S. Unstable variation compromises the location-chart limits. Software error: entering sample size as the number defective. For P and U charts, verify the response and opportunity columns are assigned to the correct boxes. Limit error: drawing specification limits as control limits. Specifications come from design or customer requirements; control limits come from process behavior. Chronology error: sorting values from low to high. Control charts require production order. Sorting by magnitude destroys the time pattern. Phase I error: deleting every red point. Exclude a point only after identifying and documenting a credible special cause. Mixed-product error: placing unlike products on one I-MR chart. Use separate charts, stages, or a Z-MR short-run approach with validated product targets. False-alarm error: turning on every test automatically. Additional tests increase sensitivity and the chance of false signals. Follow a documented monitoring plan. Capability error: calculating Cpk on an unstable process. Capability estimates are unreliable when the process distribution changes over time.

Correct chart: U chart. Why: the response is a count of defects, multiple defects can occur on one coil, and inspection opportunity varies. sections.heading: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: Lean Six Sigma Your customer sets the goalposts. Your process kicks the ball. Process capability measures — with two simple numbers, C p and C pk — whether your process can reliably land inside those goalposts. Why this matters at work: capability indices are the standard language between suppliers and customers. A contract that says “maintain C pk ≥ 1.33” is a precise, testable promise about defect rates — and knowing how to compute and read these numbers is a core skill for quality roles and a guaranteed topic on the ASQ CSSBB and CQE exams.

sections.heading: Voice of the process — the natural spread
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
Two voices: the customer and the process
Voice of the process — the natural spread
sections.text: The process doesn’t care what the drawing says. It produces values with its own mean μ and standard deviation σ. For a stable, roughly normal process, essentially all output (99.73%) lands within μ ± 3σ — a natural spread that is 6σ wide . Capability is the comparison of the two widths. If the goalposts (spec width) are much wider than the ball’s scatter (6σ), nearly everything lands in-spec. If the scatter is as wide as the goalposts — or the aim is off-centre — defects follow. One sentence to remember: C p asks “is the spread small enough?” and C pk asks “is the spread small enough where the process is actually aimed ?”

sections.heading: The formulas: Cp and Cpk
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: C p = (USL − LSL) / 6σ C p is a simple ratio of the two widths: specification width on top, natural process spread underneath. C p = 1 means the goalposts and the scatter are exactly the same width — the process barely fits, with zero room for error. C p = 2 means the goalposts are twice as wide as the scatter. But C p has a blind spot: it completely ignores where the process is centred. A process aimed way off-target can still have a beautiful C p . C pk = min [ (USL − μ) / 3σ , (μ − LSL) / 3σ ] C pk fixes the blind spot. It measures the distance from the process mean to the nearest spec limit, in units of 3σ, and reports the worse side. If the process is perfectly centred, C pk = C p . The further the mean drifts toward a limit, the lower C pk falls — even while C p stays put. That gap between the two numbers is itself a diagnosis: C p high but C pk low? The spread is fine — the process is simply off-centre. Re-aim it (usually the cheap fix). Both low? The spread itself is too wide — you have a variation-reduction project on your hands (the expensive fix).

sections.heading: How to run a capability study, step by step
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
How to run a capability study, step by step
sections.text: Confirm the process is stable first. Run a control chart (see Control Charts Explained ). Capability numbers from an unstable process are fiction — the spread you measure today won’t be the spread you get tomorrow. Check the data are roughly normal. A histogram or normal probability plot is enough at this level. Strongly skewed data need a transformation or a different method before the formulas apply. Collect enough data. Aim for at least 30 measurements — 50 to 125 is better — taken across a representative stretch of production, not one lucky hour. Compute μ and σ. Use the sample mean and sample standard deviation (or an estimate from a control chart’s subgroups — that distinction becomes C pk vs P pk later). Apply the formulas. C p from the two widths; C pk from the nearest-limit distance. Interpret and act. Compare against the agreed benchmark, then diagnose: centring problem, spread problem, or both.

sections.heading: Worked example: the coffee bag line
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
Worked example: the coffee bag line
sections.text: A packing line fills 500 g coffee bags with a spec of 500 ± 6 g (LSL = 494, USL = 506). Sixty bags from a stable run give a mean of μ = 501.2 g and a standard deviation of σ = 1.5 g . Specification width: 506 − 494 = 12 g . Natural spread: 6σ = 6 × 1.5 = 9 g . C p = 12 / 9 = 1.33 . Potential looks healthy: the goalposts are a third wider than the scatter. Upper side: (506 − 501.2) / (3 × 1.5) = 4.8 / 4.5 = 1.07 . Lower side: (501.2 − 494) / 4.5 = 7.2 / 4.5 = 1.60 . C pk = min(1.07, 1.60) = 1.07 . The story the two numbers tell: the spread is fine (C p = 1.33), but the line is overfilling by 1.2 g on average, pushing output toward the upper limit and dragging C pk down to 1.07 — below the 1.33 benchmark. The fix isn’t a costly variation-reduction project; it’s re-targeting the filler back to 500 g. Centre it, and C pk rises to meet C p at 1.33 — and the overfill give-away stops too.

sections.heading: Reading the numbers
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: Common C pk benchmarks (two-sided specs, normal, stable process) C pk Roughly how many out of spec Typical reading < 1.00 More than ~2,700 ppm Not capable — the process cannot reliably hold the spec 1.00 ~2,700 ppm (centred) Barely fits — any drift creates defects immediately 1.33 ~63 ppm The classic minimum most customers require 1.67 ~0.6 ppm Strong — typical target for safety-critical characteristics 2.00 ~0.002 ppm “Six Sigma” capability with the mean on target Why 1.33? It means the nearest spec limit sits 4σ away from the mean (because 4/3 = 1.33) — a full extra σ of safety margin beyond “barely fits.” That buffer absorbs the small drifts every real process has. One more distinction you’ll meet immediately in software: C pk vs P pk . C pk uses the within-subgroup (short-term) σ estimated from a control chart; P pk uses the overall (long-term) standard deviation of all the data. P pk is usually a little lower, because long-term data picks up the small shifts between subgroups. Minitab prints both — now you know why they differ.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: Computing capability on an unstable process. If the control chart shows special causes, the σ you measured is a moving target and the index is meaningless. Stability first, capability second — always. Quoting C p when the process is off-centre. C p is blind to centring. Reporting “C p = 1.6, we’re fine” while C pk is 0.7 hides a real defect stream. Report both; act on C pk . Forcing the formulas onto non-normal data. The ppm predictions in the table assume a normal shape. Cycle-time and flatness data, for example, are often skewed — transform first or use a non-normal capability method. Confusing 6σ in the denominator with “Six Sigma” the programme. The 6σ in C p is simply the width of the natural spread. “Six Sigma quality” refers to specs sitting six standard deviations from the mean — C p = 2.0 territory.

C pk : =MIN((E2-E4)/(3*E5), (E4-E1)/(3*E5)) — returns 1.07, flagging the off-centre fill. sections.heading: Exam tips (ASQ CSSBB / CQE)
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: Memorise both formulas cold. Exam questions hand you μ, σ, LSL, USL and expect C p and C pk in under a minute. Practice until the coffee-bag example takes you 30 seconds. Know the signature patterns: C p = C pk ⇒ perfectly centred; C p > C pk ⇒ off-centre; C pk can never exceed C p . A negative C pk means the mean is outside a spec limit. One-sided specs: with only a USL, C pk = (USL − μ)/3σ and C p is undefined — a favourite exam trap. Short-term vs long-term: C p /C pk pair with within-subgroup (short-term) σ; P p /P pk with overall (long-term) σ. Questions about “which index uses which sigma” appear on both exams. Benchmarks: 1.00 ≈ 2,700 ppm, 1.33 ≈ 63 ppm, 1.67 ≈ 0.6 ppm (centred, two-sided). Knowing 1.33 ⇔ “4σ to the nearest limit” lets you re-derive the rest. Prerequisites are testable: “What must be true before a capability study?” — stability (in control) and approximate normality. Stability always comes first.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: A machining line cuts shafts to a diameter spec of 10.0 ± 0.5 mm (LSL = 9.5, USL = 10.5). A stable run gives μ = 10.1 mm and σ = 0.12 mm . Compute both indices to two decimal places. Your C p : Your C pk : Spec width = 10.5 − 9.5 = 1.0 mm; natural spread = 6 × 0.12 = 0.72 mm. C p = 1.0 / 0.72 = 1.39 . Upper side: (10.5 − 10.1) / 0.36 = 1.11; lower side: (10.1 − 9.5) / 0.36 = 1.67. C pk = min(1.11, 1.67) = 1.11 — the spread is fine, the aim is 0.1 mm high.

sections.heading: Final summary
breadcrumb: Process Capability: Will Your Process Meet the Spec?
sections.text: Capability compares the voice of the customer (spec width) with the voice of the process (6σ spread). C p = (USL − LSL) / 6σ measures potential; it ignores centring. C pk = min[(USL − μ)/3σ, (μ − LSL)/3σ] measures reality; it reports the worse side. A gap between them is a diagnosis: re-aim if only C pk is low, reduce variation if both are. Benchmarks: 1.00 barely fits, 1.33 the classic requirement, 1.67 safety-critical territory. Stability first, capability second — and check normality before trusting the ppm predictions. If you remember one thing: C p asks whether the process could fit the spec; C pk tells you whether it actually does . Report both — the gap between them tells you what to fix.

sections.heading: Validation statement and scope
sections.text: The formulas in this document were mathematically normalized to a consistent notation and checked for dimensional consistency, denominator conventions, degrees of freedom, distribution parameterization and one-sided versus two-sided use. Formula coverage Explicit examination formula families from the supplied CSSBB, CQE and CMBB handbooks. CMBB expansion Finance, advanced MSA, time series, regression, GLM, simulation, optimization, reliability growth, advanced DOE and APC. Conventions shown Population versus sample statistics, within versus overall sigma, and distribution parameter definitions. Excluded duplication Published statistical tables and chart-constant tables are referenced rather than reproduced as thousands of individual values. “Every formula” is interpreted as every distinct governing equation or calculation family relevant to the supplied handbook content. Repeated substitutions, software output calculations and individual values in statistical lookup tables are not treated as separate formulas. Where an equation depends on a study design, the required assumptions are stated.

sections.heading: Standardization, standard errors and coefficient of variation
sections.text: M04 Measure Descriptive Statistics CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} z &=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \\[3pt] SE(\bar{x}) &=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} \approx\frac{s}{\sqrt n} \\[3pt] SE(\hat p) &=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \approx\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}} \\[3pt] SE(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2) &=\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+ \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}} \end{aligned} Use: Place observations on a standardized scale and quantify sampling variability. Exam trap: A standard deviation describes individual observations; a standard error describes a statistic across repeated samples. CSSBB probability and statistics; CQE quantitative methods.

sections.heading: Crossed ANOVA gage R&R variance components
sections.text: M12 Measure MSA CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} \hat\sigma_e^2 &=MS_E \\[3pt] \hat\sigma_{PO}^2 &=\max\left(0,\frac{MS_{PO}-MS_E}{r}\right) \\[3pt] \hat\sigma_O^2 &=\max\left(0,\frac{MS_O-MS_{PO}}{pr}\right) \\[3pt] \hat\sigma_P^2 &=\max\left(0,\frac{MS_P-MS_{PO}}{or}\right) \\[3pt] \sigma_{GRR}^2 &=\sigma_e^2+\sigma_O^2+\sigma_{PO}^2 \\[3pt] \sigma_T^2 &=\sigma_{GRR}^2+\sigma_P^2 \end{aligned} Use: Separate repeatability, operator, interaction and part-to-part variation in a balanced crossed study. Exam trap: Variance components estimated below zero are normally set to zero, but the negative estimate is a signal to review the model and data. sections.heading: PTR, percent GRR, discrimination and ndc
sections.text: M13 Measure MSA CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} PTR_{5.15} &=\frac{5.15\,\sigma_{GRR}}{USL-LSL} \\[3pt] PTR_{6} &=\frac{6\,\sigma_{GRR}}{USL-LSL} \\[3pt] \%GRR_{\text{study}} &=100\frac{\sigma_{GRR}}{\sigma_T} \\[3pt] \%GRR_{\text{tolerance}} &=100\frac{6\sigma_{GRR}}{USL-LSL} \\[3pt] ndc &=1.41\frac{\sigma_P}{\sigma_{GRR}} \end{aligned} Use: Assess whether measurement variation is sufficiently small for the intended application. Exam trap: PTR may use 5.15 or 6 depending on the source or industry. Never compare results without confirming the convention. sections.text: M14 Measure Attribute MSA CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} P_o &=\frac{\text{Number of Agreements}} {\text{Number of Comparisons}} \\[3pt] \kappa &=\frac{P_o-P_e}{1-P_e} \\[5pt] p_j &=\frac{1}{Nn}\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_{ij} \\[3pt] P_i &=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}n_{ij}^2-n} {n(n-1)} \\[3pt] \bar P &=\frac{1}{N}\sum_iP_i,\qquad P_e=\sum_jp_j^2 \\[3pt] \kappa_{\text{Fleiss}} &=\frac{\bar P-P_e}{1-P_e} \end{aligned} Use: Measure agreement after removing the agreement expected by chance. sections.heading: Kendall concordance and Kendall tau-b
sections.text: M15 Measure Attribute MSA CMBB \begin{aligned} \bar R &=\frac{m(n+1)}{2} \\[3pt] S &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(R_i-\bar R)^2 \\[3pt] T_j &=\sum_g(t_{jg}^3-t_{jg}) \\[3pt] W &=\frac{12S} {m^2(n^3-n)-m\sum_jT_j} \\[5pt] \tau_b &=\frac{C-D} {\sqrt{(C+D+T_x)(C+D+T_y)}} \end{aligned} Use: Evaluate ordinal agreement or association while accounting for rank order and ties. Exam trap: Root-sum-square combination assumes independence unless covariance terms are included. CQE metrology; CMBB BoK VI.A.1 — propagation of errors.

sections.heading: Probability laws and counting rules
sections.text: A01 Analyze Probability CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} P(A^c) &=1-P(A) \\[3pt] P(A\cup B) &=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\[3pt] P(A\cap B) &=P(A)P(B\mid A) \\[3pt] P(A\cap B)\;(\text{independent}) &=P(A)P(B) \\[5pt] {}_nP_r &=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!} \\[3pt] {n\choose r} &=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!} \\[3pt] {n\choose n_1,\ldots,n_k} &=\frac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_k!} \end{aligned} Use: Construct probabilities for mutually exclusive, overlapping, conditional and independent events. Exam trap: Mutually exclusive events with nonzero probability cannot be independent. CSSBB probability; CQE quantitative methods.

sections.text: A02 Analyze Probability CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} P(B) &=\sum_{i=1}^{k}P(B\mid A_i)P(A_i) \\[3pt] P(A_j\mid B) &=\frac{P(B\mid A_j)P(A_j)} {\sum_{i=1}^{k}P(B\mid A_i)P(A_i)} \end{aligned} Use: Update source or cause probabilities after observing evidence. sections.heading: Bernoulli and binomial distributions
sections.text: A04 Analyze Discrete Distributions CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} P(X=x)_{\text{Bernoulli}} &=p^x(1-p)^{1-x}, \quad x\in\{0,1\} \\[3pt] P(X=x)_{\text{Binomial}} &={n\choose x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x} \\[3pt] E(X)&=np \\[3pt] Var(X)&=np(1-p) \end{aligned} Use: Model independent trials with a constant probability and two possible outcomes. Exam trap: A changing probability, dependent trials or more than two outcomes violates the standard binomial assumptions. CSSBB and CQE probability distributions.

sections.text: A05 Analyze Discrete Distributions CQE \begin{aligned} P(X=x)_{\text{Geometric}} &=(1-p)^{x-1}p, \quad x=1,2,\ldots \\[3pt] E(X)&=\frac{1}{p}, \qquad Var(X)=\frac{1-p}{p^2} \\[5pt] P(X=x)_{\text{NegBin}} &={x-1\choose r-1}p^r(1-p)^{x-r}, \quad x=r,r+1,\ldots \\[3pt] E(X)&=\frac{r}{p}, \qquad Var(X)=\frac{r(1-p)}{p^2} \end{aligned} Use: Model the number of trials required to obtain the first or r-th success. sections.heading: Uniform and triangular distributions
sections.text: A08 Analyze Continuous Distributions CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} f(x)_{\text{Uniform}} &=\frac{1}{b-a}, \quad a\le x\le b \\[3pt] E(X)&=\frac{a+b}{2} \\[3pt] Var(X)&=\frac{(b-a)^2}{12} \\[5pt] E(X)_{\text{Triangular}} &=\frac{a+b+c}{3} \\[3pt] Var(X)_{\text{Triangular}} &=\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-ac-bc}{18} \end{aligned} Use: Represent bounded uncertainty when all values are equally likely or when a most-likely value is available. Exam trap: The triangular parameter c is the mode and must satisfy a ≤ c ≤ b. CQE probability and risk modeling; CMBB simulation.

sections.heading: Normal and lognormal distributions
sections.text: A09 Analyze Continuous Distributions CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} f(x)_{\text{Normal}} &=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left[-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right] \\[3pt] Z &=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma} \\[5pt] \ln X &\sim N(\mu_L,\sigma_L^2) \\[3pt] E(X)_{\text{Lognormal}} &=e^{\mu_L+\sigma_L^2/2} \\[3pt] Var(X)_{\text{Lognormal}} &=\left(e^{\sigma_L^2}-1\right) e^{2\mu_L+\sigma_L^2} \end{aligned} Use: Normal for symmetric continuous variation; lognormal for positive right-skewed multiplicative data. Exam trap: The lognormal μ and σ are parameters of ln(X), not the mean and standard deviation of X itself. CSSBB and CQE continuous distributions.

sections.heading: Exponential and Weibull distributions
sections.text: A10 Analyze Reliability Distributions CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} f(t)_{\text{Exponential}} &=\lambda e^{-\lambda t} \\[3pt] R(t)&=e^{-\lambda t} \\[3pt] F(t)&=1-e^{-\lambda t} \\[3pt] MTTF&=\frac{1}{\lambda} \\[5pt] F(t)_{\text{Weibull}} &=1-\exp\left[-\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^\beta\right] \\[3pt] R(t) &=\exp\left[-\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^\beta\right] \\[3pt] h(t) &=\frac{\beta}{\eta} \left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{\beta-1} \\[3pt] MTTF &=\eta\Gamma\left(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\right) \end{aligned} Use: Model time to failure, including decreasing, constant and increasing hazard behavior. Exam trap: β<1 indicates decreasing hazard, β=1 constant hazard and β>1 increasing hazard. CQE reliability; CSSBB capability distributions; CMBB nonnormal capability and reliability.

sections.heading: Gamma and beta distributions
sections.text: A11 Analyze Continuous Distributions CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} f(x)_{\text{Gamma}} &=\frac{x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x/\theta}} {\Gamma(\alpha)\theta^\alpha}, \quad x>0 \\[3pt] E(X)&=\alpha\theta, \qquad Var(X)=\alpha\theta^2 \\[5pt] f(x)_{\text{Beta}} &=\frac{x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}} {B(\alpha,\beta)}, \quad 0<x<1 \\[3pt] E(X)&=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta} \\[3pt] Var(X) &=\frac{\alpha\beta} {(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)} \end{aligned} Use: Gamma for positive waiting-time variables and beta for bounded proportions or probabilities. Exam trap: Gamma distributions may be parameterized with scale θ or rate λ=1/θ. Confirm which parameterization is being used. CQE probability distributions; CMBB simulation applications.

sections.text: A19 Analyze Regression CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} \hat y &=b_0+b_1x \\[3pt] b_1 &=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)} {\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2} \\[3pt] b_0 &=\bar y-b_1\bar x \\[3pt] SST &=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2 \\[3pt] SSE &=\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2 \\[3pt] SSR &=\sum_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2 \\[3pt] R^2 &=\frac{SSR}{SST} =1-\frac{SSE}{SST} \end{aligned} Use: Model a continuous response as a linear function of one predictor. sections.text: A22 Analyze Advanced Regression CSSBB CQE CMBB \begin{aligned} VIF_j &=\frac{1}{1-R_j^2} \\[3pt] h_{ii} &=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T (\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1} \mathbf x_i \\[3pt] r_i &=\frac{e_i}{s\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}} \\[3pt] D_i &=\frac{e_i^2}{p\,MSE} \frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2} \\[3pt] PRESS &=\sum_i \left(\frac{e_i}{1-h_{ii}}\right)^2 \\[3pt] R_{\text{pred}}^2 &=1-\frac{PRESS}{SST} \\[3pt] C_p^{\text{Mallows}} &=\frac{SSE_p}{MSE_{\text{full}}} -n+2p \end{aligned} Use: Diagnose multicollinearity, high leverage, influential observations and weak predictive models. lessons.title: Little’s Law
lessons.description: Watch work move through a live system, connect WIP to flow time, and explore Little’s Law in Lean and queueing theory.
keywords: little’s law littles law work in process wip throughput flow time cycle time lead time queueing theory m/m/1 lean kanban intermediate interactive

sections.heading: Little’s Law
sections.text: Learn the simple relationship that connects work in process, flow rate, and time—then watch it come alive in a production flow, a Lean value stream, and a queue. Why this matters at work: Little’s Law turns three measurements you can observe into one practical constraint. It helps teams estimate lead time, set sensible WIP limits, understand congestion, and ask better questions about why work is taking so long. Foundation

sections.heading: What is Little’s Law?
sections.text: Little’s Law describes average flow through any system with a clear entrance and exit. It says that the average number of items inside equals the average rate at which items flow through multiplied by the average time each item spends inside . The “items” can be parts, customers, patients, orders, calls, support tickets, or software tasks. The law does not predict the journey of one particular item. It connects three averages measured across many items and over time. THE FLOW RELATIONSHIP L = λ × W Average items in the system = average arrival rate × average time each item spends in the system. Think of it as a conservation rule More items arriving, or items staying longer, means more items accumulate inside the same system boundary. This is an accounting relationship—a constraint on the averages—not a claim that one variable alone caused another to change. L Average number in system Customers, parts, orders, tickets, jobs, patients, calls, etc. λ Average arrival rate Items entering per unit time. W Average time in system Waiting time + processing/service time inside the chosen boundary. Start by drawing the system boundary. An item begins contributing to L when it crosses the entrance and stops when it crosses the exit. Its W is every moment between those two events—including waiting, transport, inspection, rework, or service that happens inside the boundary. L, λ, and W must describe the same items, boundary, and observation period. Keep the units compatible. If λ is measured in parts per hour, W must be expressed in hours. For example, 20 customers/hour × 0.25 hour/customer = 5 customers in the system on average.
