sections.heading: Why the equation makes sense
sections.text: Imagine adding up every minute contributed by every item while it is inside the boundary. You can view that total two ways: as the average number present over time, or as the number of items flowing through multiplied by their average residence time. Both views count the same accumulated item-time, which is why L = λW. Interactive 1

sections.heading: Little’s Law in Lean: connect WIP to flow time
breadcrumb: Little’s Law in Lean: connect WIP to flow time
sections.text: Lean uses different operational words for the same three quantities: L becomes average work in process (WIP) , λ becomes throughput , and W becomes average flow time . In a sufficiently stable value stream, average arrivals and average completions balance, so throughput can stand in for the arrival rate. Lean / Factory Physics form WIP = Throughput × Flow Time Flow Time = WIP ÷ Throughput When the process is observed in a sufficiently stable operating regime, arrival rate and departure throughput balance, so the equation is commonly written using throughput.

sections.heading: How to read the visual
breadcrumb: Little’s Law in Lean: connect WIP to flow time
sections.text: The orange numbered tiles picture the average work occupying the chosen value stream. Set throughput and WIP, then read the calculated flow time. Press Halve WIP or Double WIP to see the mathematical effect while throughput is held fixed. Throughput: 8 parts/hour The average number of finished parts leaving per hour—not the theoretical maximum capacity. Average WIP: 24 parts All started-but-not-finished work inside the value-stream boundary. CALCULATED AVERAGE FLOW TIME 3.00 h 24 ÷ 8 = 3.00 hours Why Lean cares about WIP At the same throughput, less average WIP mathematically means less average time in the system. This is why Kanban WIP limits can be powerful. But do not misuse the equation Reducing WIP does not guarantee throughput stays fixed. An excessively low WIP limit can starve downstream work. Little’s Law constrains the averages; it does not by itself tell you which operational change caused them. Capacity, batching, rework, downtime, priorities, and variation can all change the operating point. Use process knowledge to explain the cause. Lean example A value stream averages 24 units of WIP and completes 6 units/hour . Flow time = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 hours If the team can sustainably reduce WIP to 12 while maintaining 6 units/hour, the average flow time becomes 2 hours. Interactive 3

For the waiting line alone, the matching form is Lq = λWq . The boundary determines which number-and-time pair belongs together. Queueing theory: Little’s Law works across the whole queue For the system boundary shown below, L includes customers waiting plus customers in service , and W includes waiting time plus service time .

How to read the queue visual
sections.text: λ is the arrival rate; μ is the server’s average service capacity. The purple dots approximate average queue length Lq . The blue server represents service capacity. ρ = λ/μ is utilization—the average fraction of time the server is busy in this model. L = Lq + ρ and W = Wq + 1/μ for this one-server model. Begin at λ = 10 and μ = 14. Then raise λ toward μ. Notice that the waiting measures grow nonlinearly even though the arrival rate moves in equal steps. Arrival rate λ: 10 /hour Server rate μ: 14 /hour UTILIZATION ρ = λ / μ 71.4% Arrivals → SERVER μ → Departures AVG. IN SYSTEM L 2.50 AVG. TIME W 15.0 min AVG. WAIT Wq 10.7 min AVG. QUEUE Lq 1.79 Little’s Law check: 10/hour × 0.25 hour = 2.50 Important: the extra formulas here are M/M/1 formulas, not Little’s Law This demonstration assumes one server, Poisson arrivals, exponential service times and λ < μ. Under those assumptions, W = 1/(μ − λ). Little’s Law then links the resulting averages through L = λW. Try pushing utilization toward 100% As λ approaches μ, the M/M/1 model predicts a rapidly increasing queue and waiting time. At λ ≥ μ there is no finite steady-state average queue: arrivals are entering at least as fast as the server can sustainably remove them. Go broader

sections.heading: One law, many kinds of flow
breadcrumb: One law, many kinds of flow
sections.text: The vocabulary changes by industry, but the structure does not: define a boundary, identify what flows, measure how many are inside on average, measure the rate, and measure complete time inside. Factory L: parts in WIP λ: completions per hour W: start-to-finish flow time Call centre L: callers waiting or served λ: calls admitted per hour W: wait plus talk time Hospital department L: patients present λ: patient arrivals per hour W: total department time Software delivery L: started-not-done work items λ: completions per week W: work-item lead time Order fulfilment L: open orders λ: shipments per day W: order-to-ship time Support team L: open tickets λ: resolved tickets per day W: open-to-resolution time The most useful practical rearrangement is W = L ÷ λ. If a team has 40 open items and finishes 10 per week, the implied average time in the defined system is 4 weeks. That result is a diagnostic starting point: the law tells you what the averages require, while investigation tells you whether queues, handoffs, rework, downtime, or priorities created that operating point.

sections.heading: Apply it correctly
breadcrumb: One law, many kinds of flow
sections.text: Use one consistent system boundary and one consistent item population. Use the effective or admitted arrival rate when requests can be rejected, abandoned, or cancelled. Match time units and observe long enough for meaningful averages. Do not substitute today’s snapshot for average WIP. Define “flow time,” “lead time,” and “cycle time” locally; teams do not always use those words the same way. Guided practice

sections.heading: History, limits, and references
sections.text: Little’s Law began in queueing and operations research, but later work showed why its core accounting logic reaches beyond any one probability model or industry. History and deeper interpretation John D. C. Little published the first general queueing-theory proof in 1961. Shaler Stidham later gave a deterministic sample-path treatment, showing that the underlying relationship is broader than a particular probability distribution or queue discipline. Advanced finite-window note L = Λ × w For a finite observation window T, the linked article defines Λ = N/T, where N counts every distinct item present during any part of the window—including items already inside when the window starts. It defines w as the average portion of each item’s residence time that falls inside that window. Those observer-relative quantities differ from the long-run λ and W, yet their product equals the exact time-average L for the window. This is useful when a process is changing or the reporting window is short relative to the time work spends in the system. References Krishna Kumar. A Deep Dive into Little’s Law , The Presence Calculus Project. Requested lesson reference. J. D. C. Little. “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW.” Operations Research , Vol. 9, No. 3, 1961, pp. 383–387. S. Stidham. “A Last Word on L = λW.” Operations Research , 1972. W. J. Hopp & M. L. Spearman. Factory Physics: Foundations of Manufacturing Management , 2nd ed., McGraw-Hill, 2000. One-line memory aid Stuff in the system = Stuff per unit time × Time in the system.

sections.heading: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: 6 interactives Excel Minitab ASQ CSSBB / CQE OEE is three numbers multiplied together, which makes it look easy. The hard part is deciding which bucket a loss belongs in—and two of the eight losses get put in the wrong bucket so often that entire improvement programmes end up aimed at the wrong problem. Why this matters at work: OEE does not just measure a machine. It routes your improvement effort. Call a loss "availability" when it is really "performance" and you will buy a faster changeover cart when what you needed was a jam-free infeed. The total OEE reads identically either way, which is exactly why the mistake survives for years.

Bring your own data if you can. Every interactive here starts with a realistic default, but each one accepts your numbers. A single real shift from your own line will teach you more than the worked example.

sections.heading: The three factors
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: OEE asks one question in three parts: of the time we planned to make good parts, how much actually produced good parts at full rate? OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality The three OEE factors and what each one is actually asking. Factor Question it answers Formula Availability Did the machine run when we wanted it to? Run Time ÷ Planned Production Time Performance While running, did it run at full speed? (Ideal Cycle Time × Total Count) ÷ Run Time Quality Of what it made, how much was good first time? Good Count ÷ Total Count Two definitions do most of the work, and nearly every argument about OEE is really an argument about one of them: Planned Production Time is all time minus time you genuinely did not intend to produce—no orders, unstaffed shift, planned shutdown. It is not "all time minus everything that went wrong". Ideal Cycle Time is the fastest sustainable rate the equipment has actually demonstrated for that product. Use the nameplate figure and performance will read artificially low forever. A useful mental model. Picture three filters stacked in a funnel. Planned time goes in the top. Availability strains out the time the machine was stopped, performance strains out the time it ran slow, quality strains out the parts that were not sellable. What drips out the bottom is fully productive time —time that produced a good part at full rate.

sections.heading: Terminology and calculations
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: Core terms used when measuring and reporting OEE. Term Meaning Interpretation All Time Every hour on the calendar. The denominator for TEEP, not for OEE. Planned Production Time All time minus periods you did not intend to produce. The OEE denominator. Contested more than any other term. Run Time Planned production time minus logged downtime. Only recorded stops reduce it. This is the crux of the whole lesson. Ideal Cycle Time Fastest sustainable time per part actually demonstrated. Use observed best, not nameplate, or performance is permanently understated. Total Count All parts produced, good and bad. Excludes test pieces made during changeover. Good Count Parts meeting specification first pass. Reworked parts are not good count, even if they eventually ship. Fully Productive Time Good Count × Ideal Cycle Time. The only time that fully counted. OEE is this over planned production time. Logging Threshold Shortest stop the system records, often 2–5 minutes. Decides whether a short stop lands in availability or performance. TEEP OEE × Utilisation. Measures the asset against the calendar rather than the schedule.

sections.text: Nakajima's TPM framework names eight equipment losses. Six are the familiar "six big losses"; the full eight split out tool changes and planned shutdown, which matters because those are where disputes start. Select any loss to see where it lands and why. The eight TPM losses mapped to the three OEE factors. # Loss Factor Typical evidence in the data 1 Breakdown / equipment failure Availability A logged stop with a work order behind it 2 Setup and adjustment Availability Changeover start to first good part 3 Tool, die or blade change Availability A logged stop on a predictable interval 4 Start-up and yield loss Quality Scrap concentrated in the first parts after a start 5 Minor stoppages and idling Performance Nothing in the downtime log, but the count is short 6 Reduced speed Performance Cycle time consistently above ideal 7 Defects and rework Quality Scrap spread across the run 8 Planned shutdown Availability or excluded Scheduled maintenance, no-demand time Loss 8 is a policy choice, not a fact. If planned shutdown sits inside planned production time it depresses availability. If it is excluded, availability rises and you are measuring OEE rather than TEEP. Neither is wrong. What is wrong is switching between the two and then comparing the numbers.

sections.heading: Small stops feel like availability, but they are performance
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
The two arguments that never end
Small stops feel like availability, but they are performance
sections.text: A jam is a stop. The machine is not moving. Every instinct says availability. So why is loss 5 a performance loss? Because of how the data are collected. Most downtime systems only capture stops above a threshold—commonly five minutes, sometimes two. A thirty-second jam that an operator clears by hand never becomes a downtime record. Nobody writes it down. That has a direct arithmetic consequence. If the stop is not logged, it is not subtracted from run time. The clock keeps counting the machine as running . But no parts came out during those thirty seconds. So at the end of the shift the machine is credited with 370 minutes of run time and produced only 320 parts against an ideal of 370. The shortfall has nowhere else to go: it lands in performance. The short version: small stops are invisible to the downtime log, so they can only ever show up as a rate deficit. A loss the clock never saw cannot reduce availability.

sections.heading: Setup feels like performance, but it is availability
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
The two arguments that never end
Setup feels like performance, but it is availability
sections.text: During a changeover the machine is far from idle. Operators jog the drive, run test pieces, tweak guides, make a part, measure it, adjust again. It looks like a machine running badly. Every instinct says performance. But setup has something small stops do not: a clean start and a clean end. The changeover begins when the last good part of the old order comes off and ends when the first good part of the new order is confirmed. That is a bounded, recordable event—and it goes into the downtime log as a single entry. Logged time comes out of run time, so it reduces availability. The test pieces made during setup are not counted as production. They were never sellable parts; they were part of the changeover.

sections.heading: The trick: logged or lost?
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: You do not need to memorise eight rows of a table. One question resolves every case, including both of the hard ones above.
sections.excerpt: You do not need to memorise eight rows of a table. One question resolves every case, including both of the hard ones above.

sections.heading: Ask: did the clock stop?
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: Time LOGGED as a stop → Availability Time LOST inside run time → Performance Time spent, but the part is not sellable → Quality Logged means somebody or some sensor recorded a start and an end—the event has a duration you could point at on a timeline. Lost means the time disappeared inside a period the system still counts as running, detectable only because fewer parts came out than should have. Run the two hard cases through it: Setup and adjustment. Does it have a recorded start and end? Yes—every changeover does. Logged → availability. That the machine moves during setup is irrelevant; movement was never the test. Minor stoppages. Does a thirty-second jam have a recorded start and end? No. Lost → performance. That the machine stopped is irrelevant; stopping was never the test either. The sharpest part of this trick is also its catch. Classification depends on your data collection , not on physics. Install sensors that log every jam down to five seconds and small stops genuinely become availability losses—correctly so. What you must never do is log them and also count them as performance loss. That double-counts, and the two OEE formulas will stop agreeing.

Anything you shift between availability and performance leaves OEE untouched—algebraically, not approximately.

sections.heading: How to calculate OEE for a shift
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
How to calculate OEE for a shift
sections.text: Fix the boundary. Write down planned production time first. Subtract only periods you never intended to produce. Do this before looking at any loss data, so the denominator is not quietly negotiated later. Establish ideal cycle time. Take the fastest rate the line has actually sustained for that product, evidenced from run data. Record where the number came from. Pull the downtime log. Total the logged stops. This is your availability loss, in minutes. Classify every entry. Apply logged-or-lost to each reason code. Confirm nothing is counted twice. Count production. Total count, then good count. Reworked parts are not good count. Convert to minutes. Compute performance loss and quality loss as minutes, not percentages. Reconcile. The four buckets must sum to planned production time. If they do not, stop and find the error before reporting anything. Calculate twice. A × P × Q, then the one-line formula. They must agree.

sections.heading: 1. Put everything in minutes
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: Percentages are hard to reason about and easy to mis-multiply. Minutes are not. Convert every loss into lost minutes and the whole shift reconciles on one line: Planned Production Time = Availability loss + Performance loss + Quality loss + Fully productive time Availability loss = logged downtime Performance loss = Run Time − (Total Count × Ideal Cycle Time) Quality loss = (Total Count − Good Count) × Ideal Cycle Time Fully productive time = Good Count × Ideal Cycle Time If those four do not add to planned production time you have a data error—usually a stop counted twice, or an ideal cycle time that does not match the product mix.

breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: You never actually need the three factors to get OEE: OEE = (Good Count × Ideal Cycle Time) ÷ Planned Production Time This is the best check you have. sections.heading: 3. Attack your weakest factor first

sections.text: Because the three multiply, the gain from improving one factor by a point is the product of the other two: ∂OEE / ∂A = P × Q The lowest factor always has the highest product of the other two, so it always returns the most OEE per point. That is a mathematical result, not a rule of thumb—and the next interactive lets you confirm it.

breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: 90 %, 90 % and 90 % do not average to 90 %. They multiply to 72.9 % . Three respectable numbers make one poor one. The widely quoted "world class" 85 % is 90.0 × 95.0 × 99.9—note how little quality loss it tolerates.

sections.text: Moving availability from 80 % to 82 % is two percentage points , and a 2.5 % relative improvement. "We improved availability by 2 %" is ambiguous and will be challenged in any serious review.

sections.heading: 6. Performance above 100 % means your ideal is wrong
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
6. Performance above 100 % means your ideal is wrong
sections.text: Performance is capped at 1.0 by definition. If you compute 104 %, the ideal cycle time is too slow, the part count includes rework passes, or run time is understated. Fix the input; never cap the output. Exam habit. Write the four time buckets before touching a calculator. Most OEE questions on the CSSBB and CQE test whether you put each stated loss in the right bucket, not whether you can divide.

sections.heading: Worked example
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: A single shift on a packaging line. These are the calculator defaults, so you can follow along above. Shift inputs for the worked example. Input Value Shift length 480 min Planned stops (breaks, handover) 30 min Planned Production Time 450 min Logged downtime (breakdown 25, setup 40, tool change 15) 80 min Run Time 370 min Ideal cycle time 1.0 min/part Total parts made 320 Rejects (8 start-up, 4 process) 12 Good parts 308 Availability = 370 / 450 = 0.8222 = 82.22 % Performance = (1.0 × 320) / 370 = 0.8649 = 86.49 % Quality = 308 / 320 = 0.9625 = 96.25 % OEE = 0.8222 × 0.8649 × 0.9625 = 0.6844 = 68.44 % Check with the one-line formula: OEE = (308 × 1.0) / 450 = 0.6844 = 68.44 % ✓ Check with the time buckets: Availability loss = 80 min Performance loss = 370 − 320 = 50 min Quality loss = 12 × 1.0 = 12 min Fully productive = 308 × 1.0 = 308 min Total = 450 min ✓ Note what the buckets reveal that the percentages hide. The largest single loss is not the breakdown everyone talks about—it is the 50 minutes of performance loss, which nobody logged and nobody raised at the morning meeting. It is invisible precisely because it never reached the downtime report. The same shift, classified differently. Suppose 30 of those 50 performance minutes are the sixty small stops. Log them and availability falls to 75.56 % while performance rises to 94.12 %—and OEE stays at 68.44 %. Read the first version and you chase breakdowns and changeovers. Read the second and you see the real problem is sixty jams a shift, which is an infeed project, not a maintenance one. The number was never wrong. The diagnosis was.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: Using nameplate speed as ideal cycle time. Performance is then permanently depressed and no improvement ever shows. Counting rework as good. Quality means good first pass . A part needing a second operation is a quality loss even if it eventually ships. Moving unplanned events into planned stops. Reclassifying a breakdown as "planned downtime" inflates OEE and hides the problem. Planned means you intended it before the shift started. Comparing OEE across different machines. OEE compares a machine to itself over time. Cross-machine league tables reward whoever set the softest ideal cycle time. Double-counting a logged small stop. Once it is in the downtime log it is an availability loss. Counting it again as performance loss breaks the reconciliation. Optimising OEE on a non-bottleneck. Running a non-constraint at high OEE builds inventory, not throughput. Reporting OEE without the loss breakdown. A single percentage tells nobody what to do next. Always publish the four buckets alongside it.

breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: Reason-code roll-up. With stop reasons in column B and minutes in column C, =SUMIFS($C:$C,$B:$B,"Setup") gives setup minutes. Repeat for all eight losses and confirm the total equals your logged downtime—if it does not, reason codes are missing or overlapping. Frequency versus duration. Put =COUNTIFS($B:$B,"Minor stop") beside =SUMIFS($C:$C,$B:$B,"Minor stop") . This separates "one long jam" from "sixty short ones", which demand completely different countermeasures and look identical in a minutes total. How much is invisible? =COUNTIFS(durations,"<"&$B$1) against your threshold in B1 counts the stops your system never records—the Excel equivalent of the threshold interactive above. Demonstrated ideal cycle time. Instead of arguing about nameplate speed, take =PERCENTILE.INC(cycle_times, 0.05) across clean runs. The fifth percentile of observed cycles is a defensible "fastest sustained" figure. Reconciliation column. Add =PPT-(down+perf_loss+qual_loss+productive) . It should read zero on every row. Any non-zero cell is a data problem, and finding it here is far cheaper than in a review meeting. Mixed-model shifts. =SUMPRODUCT(part_counts, ideal_times) gives total ideal minutes when several products with different cycle times ran in one shift.

sections.heading: Minitab navigation
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: Minitab menu paths for OEE analysis, with guidance on which option to choose. Task Menu path Which option and why Rank the eight losses Stat → Quality Tools → Pareto Chart Run it twice—once on stop count , once on stop minutes . Minor stops usually top the count chart and barely register on the minutes chart, which is the entire argument for treating them separately. Trend OEE over time Graph → Time Series Plot → Simple Use before any control chart. Shift patterns and changeover effects are usually visible by eye and tell you whether a control chart is even appropriate. Is OEE stable? Stat → Control Charts → Variables Charts for Individuals → I-MR Daily OEE is one value per period, so individuals is the right family. Alternative: Variables Charts for Subgroups → Xbar-R when you have several lines per shift and want between-line variation separated. Did an improvement work? Stat → Basic Statistics → 2-Sample t Compares mean OEE before and after. Check normality first via Stat → Basic Statistics → Normality Test; OEE is a bounded ratio and skews badly near the top of its range. Non-normal OEE data Stat → Nonparametrics → Mann-Whitney Use when the normality test fails or the sample is small. Compares medians and assumes no distribution. Which loss drives OEE? Stat → Regression → Regression → Fit Regression Model OEE as response, loss minutes by category as predictors. Exploratory only—the predictors are compositional and not independent, so read coefficients as direction, not effect size. Stop duration distribution Graph → Histogram → With Fit Reveals the threshold effect directly. A gap just below your logging threshold is evidence that small stops are being missed rather than genuinely absent. Compare lines or shifts Stat → ANOVA → One-Way Use when comparing three or more lines. Follow with Tukey comparisons to see which pairs actually differ rather than eyeballing the means.

sections.heading: Exam tips
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: Classification is the question. CSSBB and CQE items normally list shift events and ask for OEE. The arithmetic is trivial; the marks are in bucketing each event. Apply logged-or-lost to every line before calculating. Watch for planned time traps. A stem mentioning "two 15-minute breaks and a 30-minute unplanned stoppage" is testing whether you subtract the breaks from planned production time and leave the stoppage as an availability loss. Rework is a quality loss. If a stem says parts "required rework before shipping", they are not good count. One of the most common single-mark errors. Know the one-line formula. Faster than three divisions and it self-checks. Learn it as the primary method and use A × P × Q to confirm. OEE versus TEEP. If a question introduces total calendar time or unstaffed shifts, it is testing utilisation: TEEP = OEE × Utilisation. Reclassification questions. If a stem changes the logging threshold and asks what happens to OEE, the answer is "nothing"—availability and performance move in opposite directions by design. In the real world. Expect to defend your ideal cycle time more than your arithmetic. Bring the demonstrated-rate evidence; "the nameplate says so" will not survive review.

sections.heading: Final summary
breadcrumb: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Eight Losses
sections.text: OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality , and the one-line form (Good Count × Ideal Cycle Time ÷ Planned Production Time) gives the same answer as a check. The eight TPM losses map to three factors. Breakdown, setup, tool change and planned shutdown are availability; minor stops and reduced speed are performance; defects and start-up losses are quality. Logged or lost resolves any classification. Recorded time reduces availability, time that vanishes inside run time surfaces as performance, unsellable output is quality. Minor stops are a performance loss because nothing records them , not because of anything physical. Setup is an availability loss because it is recorded, not because the machine is still. Run time cancels in A × P , so classification never changes total OEE. It changes which improvement project you start—which is why it matters. Reconcile every shift in minutes. The four buckets must sum to planned production time. Improve your weakest factor first. The marginal gain is the product of the other two.

sections.heading: Short-Run SPC: Control Charts for High-Mix, Low-Volume Processes
breadcrumb: Short-Run SPC: Control Charts for High-Mix, Low-Volume Processes
sections.text: Intermediate 50 minutes Interactive Excel and Minitab guidance Learn how to monitor one common process while products, grades, gauges, targets, and normal variation keep changing—an intermediate Lean Six Sigma application of statistical process control. You will transform mixed-product data, qualify valid product families, and select the correct short-run chart without mistaking planned product changes for process instability. Why this matters at work: a conventional chart of raw values can signal every time the mill changes product. Separate charts can be equally weak when each product appears only a few times. Short-run SPC creates one statistically meaningful process view by removing the changes that were supposed to happen.

sections.heading: Why short-run charts exist
breadcrumb: Short-Run SPC: Control Charts for High-Mix, Low-Volume Processes
sections.text: A conventional control chart works best when the plotted values come from one stable process condition. In a high-mix operation, however, a schedule may look like this: Production sequence: 8.2 mm → 7.8 mm → 8.4 mm → 8.2 mm → 10.0 mm → 7.8 mm. The target changes are intentional; the question is whether the process is hitting each target consistently.

sections.heading: The short-run solution
breadcrumb: Short-Run SPC: Control Charts for High-Mix, Low-Volume Processes
sections.text: Translate each result into a common statistical language before charting it. You can subtract the product target, divide by the product standard deviation, or compare the observed count with its product-specific expected count. The transformed stream then answers: Core question: after accounting for what was supposed to change between products, is the shared process behaving consistently over time? What short-run SPC does not do: it does not make unrelated processes comparable, replace engineering judgment, or turn specification limits into control limits.

sections.heading: Key terminology
breadcrumb: Short-Run SPC: Control Charts for High-Mix, Low-Volume Processes
sections.text: Term Plain-language meaning Practical interpretation Short run A small quantity of one product before the process changes to another product. The chart may run for years; the individual product campaigns are short. Process stream The common equipment, method, measurement system, and causal mechanism being monitored. Products may differ, but they must still be generated by a defensibly common process. Product family A group of products similar enough to share a short-run baseline or transformation. Same mill alone is not enough; route, control mechanism, measurement, and variation matter. Nominal or target The intended value for a specific product. Subtract it to remove planned differences in product center. Deviation from nominal Actual result minus that product's target. Positive means above target; negative means below target. Standardized value Deviation expressed in units of that product's standard deviation. A value of +2 is two product-specific standard deviations above expectation. Homogeneity of variance Products have sufficiently similar natural process variation. Required for simple DNOM/X-nominal pooling; otherwise standardize or separate. Historical parameter A validated mean, target, standard deviation, or baseline rate estimated before monitoring. It must come from stable, representative data—not a mixture already containing special causes. Rational subgroup Measurements grouped so within-subgroup variation represents short-term variation. Examples include several thickness readings across one coil or repeated specimens under one condition.

sections.heading: Interactive: can these products share one short-run chart?
breadcrumb: Short-Run SPC: Control Charts for High-Mix, Low-Volume Processes
Interactive: can these products share one short-run chart?
sections.text: Short-run SPC begins with engineering qualification, not a formula. Check the statements that are true for the proposed product family. Same process route: the products pass through the same relevant equipment and control strategy. Same measurement system: method, location, resolution, calibration, and units are comparable. Same physical mechanism: the response is controlled by comparable metallurgical or mechanical behaviour. Comparable sampling logic: individual values or rational subgroups mean the same thing across products. Stable product baselines: targets, means, standard deviations, or rates come from stable history. Common response to special causes: sensor drift, roll wear, or cooling problems would affect products in a comparable direction. Product standard deviations are… Known process break between products? Result: complete the checks, then evaluate. Steel-mill example: body Charpy, HAZ Charpy, and weld-metal Charpy may share joules as a unit, but they do not automatically share one physical process distribution. Standardizing unlike mechanisms can hide rather than solve the problem.

sections.heading: Interactive: screen for comparable variation
breadcrumb: Short-Run SPC: Control Charts for High-Mix, Low-Volume Processes
sections.text: The source flowchart asks whether product standard deviations are equal. In practice, use stable product-specific estimates, engineering judgment, graphical comparison, and—where appropriate—a formal equal-variance analysis. This quick ratio is a screening diagnostic only , not a universal acceptance test. Product A standard deviation Product B standard deviation Product C standard deviation Product D standard deviation, optional Largest σ 0.039 Smallest σ 0.035 Max / min ratio 1.11 Screening result: similar enough to investigate a difference-from-nominal chart, subject to stable data and engineering review. Interpret the ratio cautiously: near 1 means similar estimates. A ratio above about 1.5 deserves closer review; above 2 usually makes simple pooled DNOM limits difficult to defend. Sample size, uncertainty, practical units, and product physics still control the final decision.

sections.heading: A defensible short-run SPC implementation procedure
breadcrumb: Short-Run SPC: Control Charts for High-Mix, Low-Volume Processes
A defensible short-run SPC implementation procedure
sections.text: Define the monitoring question. Decide whether you are monitoring one product or the health of a common process across many products. Preserve time order. Arrange observations by actual production or test sequence. Product order is not a substitute for time order. Define the process stream. Specify equipment, route, operating mechanism, measurement system, test location, and subgroup logic. Form candidate product families. Use engineering knowledge before statistical pooling. Document exclusions and known process breaks. Validate historical baselines. Estimate targets, expected means, standard deviations, ranges, or defect rates from stable and representative periods. Choose the coding method. Use deviation from nominal only when product variation is comparable; otherwise standardize. Select the chart family. Follow variables versus attributes, individuals versus subgroups, and defective units versus defect counts. Build Phase I limits. Use enough pooled stable subgroups to estimate the common chart behaviour, investigate signals, remove only verified special causes, and recalculate once. Freeze the baseline for Phase II. Monitor new data using the validated historical parameters. Do not let every new point continuously redefine normal. Maintain traceability. Keep product, grade, gauge, heat, slab, rolling practice, test location, recipe, and equipment status available for signal investigation even though the chart plots coded values. Minimum-history principle: pooling legitimate product families helps accumulate the roughly 20 or more stable subgroups normally desired for an initial control-limit study. The pooled count does not excuse weak product-specific targets or standard deviations.

Coils 9–12 also show a sustained positive shift. Investigate gauge-control bias, roll wear, target-table changes, temperature-model drift, or measurement changes around coil 9. Phase I caution: this 12-point example teaches the calculation; it is not enough by itself to establish a permanent production baseline. A real implementation should use a larger stable historical period and recompute limits after verified special causes are addressed.

sections.text: What you see What it suggests What to investigate Raw values jump at every product change, coded values remain stable The raw chart was reacting to intended target changes. Use the coded short-run chart; keep product labels for traceability. Coded values shift above zero across several products A common positive process bias, not a single product target issue. Calibration, control-loop bias, recipe table, common sensor, roll or cooling condition. Only one product repeatedly signals after standardization Product baseline may be wrong or the family assumption may fail. Target/mean/σ estimate, route, test location, product-specific mechanism. Location chart stable; W or range chart signals Average performance is centered, but short-term variation has increased. Measurement instability, material inconsistency, control oscillation, equipment wear. DNOM chart signals mainly for products with larger σ Equal-variation assumption is likely false. Standardize by product variation or split the family. Standardized p/u value exceeds +3 Observed defect level is unexpectedly high after accounting for baseline rate and sample opportunity. Defect definition, inspection exposure, product mix, process change, inspection sensitivity. Chart stable but coded center is not zero The process may be consistently biased relative to targets. Decide whether to remove the bias, revise a technically justified target, or use a process-centered Phase II chart while preserving target performance reporting.

sections.text: Task Example Excel formula Notes Look up product target =XLOOKUP([@Product],Parameters[Product],Parameters[Target]) Keep parameters in a controlled table. Deviation from target =[@Actual]-[@Target] Preserves original unit. Standardized variable value =LET(x,[@Actual],mu,[@Mean],s,[@SD],IF(s>0,(x-mu)/s,NA())) Guard against zero or missing σ. Moving range =ABS(CurrentDeviation-PreviousDeviation) Do not bridge invalid process breaks. Average by product =AVERAGEIFS(Data[Actual],Data[Product],[@Product]) Use only validated stable baseline rows. Product standard deviation =STDEV.S(FILTER(Data[Actual],Data[Product]=[@Product])) Review sample size and stability. Standardized p =LET(p,[@Defectives]/[@n],p0,[@BaselineRate],(p-p0)/SQRT(p0*(1-p0)/[@n])) Requires 0<p0<1 and a valid sample size. Standardized u =LET(u,[@Defects]/[@Opportunity],u0,[@BaselineRate],(u-u0)/SQRT(u0/[@Opportunity])) Opportunity must use the same unit as u0. Excel mistake: do not use the entire live dataset to recalculate targets and standard deviations on every refresh. Store validated Phase II parameters separately so a new special cause does not redefine its own limits.

sections.heading: Minitab: standardized individual variables
breadcrumb: Short-Run SPC: Control Charts for High-Mix, Low-Volume Processes
sections.text: Arrange the individual measurements in one column and the product/part identifier in a second column. Choose Stat → Control Charts → Variables Charts for Individuals → Z-MR . Enter the measurement column under Variables and the product identifier under Part indicator . When validated historical means and standard deviations exist, open Z-MR Options → Parameters and supply them by part/product. Review both panels: the Z chart for location and the MR chart for changes in standardized short-term variation. For X-nominal or other custom transformations, calculate the coded statistic in the worksheet first, then chart the coded column with the appropriate ordinary I-MR or X̄-R procedure using historical parameters where applicable. Minitab output to prioritize: product/part parameter estimates, centerline and limits, tests for special causes, point labels, and whether the moving-range or range panel signals before the location panel. Minitab mistake: allowing the software to estimate each product's mean and standard deviation from sparse or unstable observations can give a mathematically complete but operationally weak chart.

sections.text: A pipe mill monitors surface indications per 1,000 m. Product family P has a stable expected rate of 0.60 indications per 1,000 m. The current run covers 2,500 m and contains 6 indications. Choose the chart family. Calculate the observed defects per 1,000 m. Calculate the standardized statistic. Decide whether the point exceeds the +3 control limit. Chart choice Observed u, defects per 1,000 m Standardized Z Answer: use a standardized u-chart because you are counting defects and the inspected opportunity varies. u = 6 defects 2.5 units of 1,000 m = 2.40 defects per 1,000 m Z u = 2.40 − 0.60 √(0.60 / 2.5) = 1.80 0.4899 = 3.67 Because 3.67 exceeds the +3 limit, the run is a special-cause signal after accounting for both the product baseline and the inspected length.

sections.heading: Final summary
breadcrumb: Short-Run SPC: Control Charts for High-Mix, Low-Volume Processes
sections.text: “Short run” refers to the limited production quantity of each product—not the operating life of the chart. Use a traditional chart when one repeatable product/process condition supplies enough sequential data. Use X-nominal or DNOM when targets differ but product variation is reasonably comparable. Use Z/W or standardized attribute charts when product-specific variation or baseline rates differ. Variables versus attributes, individual versus subgroup, defective versus defect, and constant versus varying opportunity determine the terminal chart. Qualify the process stream and product family before pooling. Common units or shared equipment are not sufficient. Control limits detect changes in the coded process; specifications still judge product acceptance. Keep complete product and process traceability so every coded signal can be investigated in engineering terms. Decision rule: first remove the product differences that should exist; then chart what remains—but only after proving the products share one meaningful process stream. Suggested next lesson: Control Charts, Explained for signal rules, followed by a process-capability lesson once stability is established.

sections.heading: ARL, 1/α, and 1/(1−β)
breadcrumb: Signal or Noise — ARL, Nelson Rules & Control Limit Design
sections.text: Every control chart rule you'll ever use is a bet against a stable, random process. Average Run Length (ARL) is how you keep score: how many points, on average, before the chart signals — under a given process condition.
sections.excerpt: Every control chart rule you'll ever use is a bet against a stable, random process. Average Run Length (ARL) is how you keep score: how many points, on average, before the chart signals — under a given process condition.

sections.heading: In-control: ARL₀ = 1/α
breadcrumb: Signal or Noise — ARL, Nelson Rules & Control Limit Design
sections.text: α is the probability that a single point falsely signals when nothing is actually wrong. For a normal distribution and a 3σ limit, α is just the tail area beyond ±3 standard deviations. α = P(Z < −3) + P(Z > 3) α = 0.00135 + 0.00135 α ≈ 0.0027 ARL₀ = 1 / α ARL₀ = 1 / 0.0027 ARL₀ ≈ 370 points Why 1/α works Each point is an independent Bernoulli trial: "signal" or "no signal," with probability α of signaling. The number of trials until the first success follows a geometric distribution , and the mean of a geometric distribution is exactly 1/p. So ARL₀ isn't a rule of thumb — it falls straight out of the geometric mean.

sections.heading: Out-of-control: ARL₁ = 1/(1−β)
breadcrumb: Signal or Noise — ARL, Nelson Rules & Control Limit Design
sections.text: β is the probability of missing a real shift on any given point — the point still falls inside the limits even though the process has moved. (1−β) is power : the chance you catch the shift on that point. Power depends entirely on how big the shift is, in σ units. Try it Drag the shift size below. Watch β and ARL₁ move together — small shifts are sneaky; big shifts get caught almost immediately. Shift size (σ units) 1.5σ Control limit width Live control chart same shift, same limit — just a fresh random path Notice the trap: β (miss probability) and ARL₁ (points-to-detect) both explode as the shift shrinks toward zero, and both collapse toward 1 as the shift grows large. There's no free lunch — sensitivity to small shifts always trades against false-alarm rate, which is exactly why the Nelson tests exist: they buy sensitivity to small/moderate shifts without touching the primary 3σ limit. Don't confuse these two lines The chart above marks two different things, and it's easy to blur them together: The shaded region starts at the control limit (±3σ from the original mean) — fixed, decided in advance, never moves . This is the chart's actual decision rule, and it's what power (1−β) is measured against. The dashed violet line marks where the two curves cross — where the shifted and original distributions have equal height. This point slides with the shift (it sits at exactly half the shift size) but it is not a decision boundary the chart uses. Sliding the "catches the shift" boundary from the control limit to the crossing point would badly overstate power — a real 0.5σ drift is only caught ~0.6% of the time at the true 3σ limit, but would look like ~60% if you measured from the crossing point instead. The crossing point is the boundary you'd use if you already knew the exact shift size ahead of time (a Neyman–Pearson-style optimal test); a real control chart can't do that because it has to watch for shifts of every possible size with one fixed rule. That constraint is exactly why the Nelson zone tests exist as a workaround, rather than the chart adapting its limit. Next: The 8 Nelson tests → PART 2

sections.heading: 2σ vs 3σ — run the simulation yourself
breadcrumb: Signal or Noise — ARL, Nelson Rules & Control Limit Design
sections.text: Don't take α ≈ 0.0455 vs 0.0027 on faith. Generate a genuinely stable, in-control process below and watch how often each limit width cries wolf. Points to simulate 370 0 FALSE ALARMS AT 3σ 0 FALSE ALARMS AT 2σ — 2σ ALARM RATE ÷ 3σ ALARM RATE Why not just tighten to 2σ? At 2σ, ARL₀ collapses to about 22 points — roughly 1 false alarm every 22 subgroups even when the process hasn't moved at all. Run this on a high-volume line (every heat, every coil) and operators either chase noise constantly or, more dangerously, learn to ignore the chart. 3σ was chosen as the economic balance: rare enough false alarms that a signal can be trusted, without waiting forever to catch real shifts.

sections.heading: The layered design
breadcrumb: Signal or Noise — ARL, Nelson Rules & Control Limit Design
sections.text: This is why real SPC systems don't just pick one limit width and stop. They keep the primary limit at 3σ (protecting ARL₀ ≈ 370) and layer the Nelson zone tests on top, each aimed at a specific shift signature the lone 3σ rule would catch too slowly. You get most of the detection speed of tighter limits without paying for it in constant false alarms — as long as you're deliberate about which tests you actually turn on (see the combined-α note below). The catch The 8 tests are calibrated individually, but they run simultaneously on every point and aren't independent of each other. Treating them as roughly independent, the combined chance that at least one test fires on a stable point is noticeably higher than any single test's α — summing the both-sides probabilities above gives roughly 2.2% per point with all 8 active (a union-bound upper estimate, since overlapping tests can't simply be added) — dragging combined ARL₀ down toward the 45–70 range. That's the real reason most production charts run a curated subset (often 1, 2, 3, 5) rather than all eight blindly. ← Back Next: CUSUM vs Shewhart → PART 4

sections.heading: CUSUM — catching small shifts faster
breadcrumb: Signal or Noise — ARL, Nelson Rules & Control Limit Design
sections.text: Every rule so far — 3σ, the Nelson zone tests — looks at a handful of recent points and forgets everything before them. A CUSUM chart (Cumulative Sum) never forgets: it adds up every deviation from target, forever, so even a shift too small to trip any single-point rule eventually accumulates into an unmistakable signal.

sections.heading: How it works
breadcrumb: Signal or Noise — ARL, Nelson Rules & Control Limit Design
sections.text: Two running sums track evidence of an upward shift (C⁺) and a downward shift (C⁻). Each resets to zero the moment it has no evidence left, but as long as the process keeps leaning one direction, it keeps climbing: C⁺ᵢ = max(0, C⁺ᵢ₋₁ + (xᵢ − target) − k) C⁻ᵢ = max(0, C⁻ᵢ₋₁ − (xᵢ − target) − k) Signal the moment C⁺ᵢ > H or C⁻ᵢ > H k (the "allowance" or reference value) is how much deviation gets forgiven each point before it counts toward the sum — conventionally set to half the shift size you most want to catch quickly (k = Δ/2). H (the decision interval) is the threshold that triggers a signal, chosen to hit a target false-alarm rate — exactly the same design decision as choosing 3σ for a Shewhart chart, just with different knobs. Matched comparison, not a rigged one To compare fairly, both charts below are tuned to the same false-alarm rate : the Shewhart chart uses the standard 3σ limit (ARL₀ ≈ 370), and this CUSUM uses k = 0.5σ with H calibrated by simulation to ARL₀ ≈ 370 as well. Any difference you see in detection speed is a real difference in power, not one chart being given an easier bar to clear.

sections.heading: The systematic result
breadcrumb: Signal or Noise — ARL, Nelson Rules & Control Limit Design
sections.text: One random draw is a story, not proof. Here's what a large simulation (thousands of trials per row, both methods calibrated to ARL₀ ≈ 370) says about the average number of points needed to catch a shift of each size: Shift size Shewhart ARL₁ (exact) CUSUM ARL₁ (simulated) CUSUM is 0.25σ 281.2 120.7 2.3× faster 0.50σ 155.2 35.0 4.4× faster 1.00σ 43.9 9.9 4.4× faster 1.50σ 15.0 5.5 2.7× faster 2.00σ 6.3 3.8 1.6× faster 3.00σ 2.0 2.5 0.8× — Shewhart wins Where CUSUM stops winning Notice the last row. For a huge, sudden jump (3σ or more), Shewhart is actually just as fast or slightly faster — a single point that extreme trips the 3σ rule almost immediately, while CUSUM still has to accumulate at least a little evidence. CUSUM's advantage is specifically for small and moderate sustained shifts — exactly the range where a Shewhart chart is weakest and the Nelson zone tests were invented to compensate. CUSUM is a different, often better, way to solve the same problem those zone tests target. ← Back Next: Summary table → PART 5

sections.heading: Key takeaways
breadcrumb: Signal or Noise — ARL, Nelson Rules & Control Limit Design
sections.text: 1 ARL is just a geometric-distribution mean. ARL₀ = 1/α (false alarms under a stable process) and ARL₁ = 1/(1−β) (points to catch a real shift) trade off against each other — tightening one always loosens the other. 2 3σ limits exist because they balance that trade-off economically: rare enough false alarms (ARL₀ ≈ 370) to trust a signal, without an unreasonable wait to catch real shifts. 3 The 8 Nelson tests each target a different failure signature (jump, drift, oscillation, moderate/small shift, stratification, mixture) by asking how surprising a run of points would be under a stable process — but running all 8 at once inflates the combined false-alarm rate well past any single test's α. 4 A control limit is a fixed decision boundary, decided before you know if or how much the process will shift. It is not the point where two hypothetical distributions cross — that's a different, shift-dependent concept. 5 CUSUM accumulates evidence across points instead of judging each one alone, making it 2–4× faster than a matched Shewhart chart at catching small/moderate sustained shifts — though Shewhart holds its own (or edges ahead) for a single huge jump.

sections.text: Function Syntax Purpose When to use it NORM.S.DIST =NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE) Standard normal CDF, Φ(z). Compute one-sided tail area beyond a control limit, e.g. =1-NORM.S.DIST(3,TRUE) for the 3σ tail (≈ 0.00135), the building block of α and ARL₀. NORM.S.INV =NORM.S.INV(probability) Inverse standard normal CDF (z from a probability). Back-solve for a control limit width given a target α, or find the crossing point between two shifted normal curves. NORM.DIST =NORM.DIST(x,mean,sd,TRUE) CDF of a normal distribution with any mean/SD. Compute β directly for a shifted process: =NORM.DIST(limit,shift,1,TRUE)-NORM.DIST(-limit,shift,1,TRUE) reproduces the β calculation used throughout Part 1. BINOM.DIST =BINOM.DIST(k,n,p,FALSE) Exact binomial point probability. Derive the Nelson zone-test probabilities (Rules 5 and 6), e.g. =BINOM.DIST(2,3,0.02275,FALSE) for "2 of 3 beyond Zone A." COMBIN =COMBIN(n,k) Number of combinations, C(n,k). Build the same zone-test binomial terms by hand instead of relying on BINOM.DIST , useful when showing the derivation step by step (as in the "Show derivation" panels above). FACT =FACT(n) Factorial, n!. Compute the trend-test denominator (6! = 720) used to derive Rule 3's P ≈ 0.0028. GEOMDIST / NEGBINOM.DIST =NEGBINOM.DIST(0,1,p,TRUE) Geometric distribution mean/CDF (Excel exposes it as a special case of the negative binomial). Confirm that ARL is exactly the geometric-distribution mean, 1/p — the identity behind ARL₀ = 1/α and ARL₁ = 1/(1−β).

sections.text: Task Menu path Notes Build a Shewhart individuals chart (3σ limits) Stat → Control Charts → Variables Charts for Individuals → I-MR Minitab plots the individuals (I) chart with 3σ limits by default and the moving-range (MR) chart alongside it — the direct equivalent of the Part 1/3 simulations. Turn on the Nelson (Western Electric) zone tests Stat → Control Charts → I-MR → I-MR Options → Tests tab Minitab lists all 8 tests by number, matching this lesson's numbering exactly, and lets you select a subset. Selecting all 8 reproduces the inflated combined-α effect discussed in Part 3 — most practitioners enable only 1, 2, 3, and 5. Tighten or loosen the control limit width Stat → Control Charts → I-MR → I-MR Options → Estimate tab (or Parameters, to fix limits manually) Minitab defaults to 3σ; to reproduce the Part 3 comparison, run the chart twice — once at the default and once with sigma limits manually set to 2 — and compare the number of flagged points. Build a CUSUM chart Stat → Control Charts → Time-Weighted Charts → CUSUM The dialog asks directly for the reference value (k, as "shift to detect" in σ or raw units) and the decision interval (H) — the same two knobs derived in Part 4. Minitab can also estimate them from a target ARL, which is how the k = 0.5σ, H ≈ 4.77 pairing in this lesson was chosen. Which option should you choose? Start from what you're trying to catch: a single Shewhart I-MR chart with a curated subset of Nelson tests (1, 2, 3, 5) covers sudden shifts, trends, and moderate sustained shifts without inflating the false-alarm rate too far past ARL₀ ≈ 370. Add a CUSUM chart specifically when the process risk is a small, slow sustained drift — exactly the case Part 4 shows Shewhart is weakest against.

sections.heading: Exam Tips
breadcrumb: Signal or Noise — ARL, Nelson Rules & Control Limit Design
sections.text: 1 ARL questions are geometric-mean questions in disguise. ASQ CSSBB/CQE items that ask "how many subgroups on average before a false alarm" are testing whether you know ARL₀ = 1/α, not a memorized constant — recompute it from the tail area if the limit width in the question isn't the standard 3σ. 2 Know which Nelson rule number matches which pattern. Exam scenarios describe a pattern in words ("nine consecutive points on one side of the centerline") and expect you to name the rule and what it detects — drift, oscillation, stratification, or a mixture — not just recite probabilities. 3 Don't confuse the control limit with the crossing point. A common exam trap describes "where the shifted and original distributions overlap" and asks you to compute power from it — the correct boundary is always the fixed control limit, never the shift-dependent crossing point. 4 CUSUM vs. Shewhart is a recurring comparison question. Remember the shape of the trade-off: CUSUM wins for small/moderate sustained shifts, Shewhart holds even or wins for one huge jump — and both are typically compared at a matched ARL₀ so the comparison is fair. 5 Combined false-alarm rate is a favorite "gotcha." If a question implies all 8 Nelson tests run simultaneously, the effective ARL₀ is well below 370 — don't answer with the single-rule 0.27% α unless the question specifies only the primary 3σ rule is active. ← Back to Summary

sections.heading: Three indices: factor A, factor B, and replicate
breadcrumb: Understanding Dot Notation in Plain English
Three indices: factor A, factor B, and replicate
sections.text: In a replicated two-factor experiment, write a measurement as \(y_{ijk}\). Define the positions first: \(i=1,\ldots,a\) identifies factor A, \(j=1,\ldots,b\) identifies factor B, and \(k=1,\ldots,n\) identifies a replicate within that A–B combination. Here, every combination has the same number \(n\) of observations. A cell means one combination of factor levels. The plain-text form y.j. means \(y_{\cdot j\cdot}\): keep B level j fixed; add over every A level and every replicate . It has three subscript positions. It is different from the two-position \(y_{\cdot j}\). The dots are placeholders for summed indices, not decimal points or multiplication signs. All dot patterns for three-index observations Notation / typed form Held fixed Explicit summation Number of values added \(y_{ijk}\) / yijk i, j, k One observation; no summation 1 \(y_{ij\cdot}\) / yij. i, j \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_{ijk}\) n \(y_{i\cdot k}\) / yi.k i, k \(\sum_{j=1}^{b}y_{ijk}\) b \(y_{\cdot jk}\) / y.jk j, k \(\sum_{i=1}^{a}y_{ijk}\) a \(y_{i\cdot\cdot}\) / yi.. i \(\sum_{j=1}^{b}\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_{ijk}\) bn \(y_{\cdot j\cdot}\) / y.j. j \(\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_{ijk}\) an \(y_{\cdot\cdot k}\) / y..k k \(\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{j=1}^{b}y_{ijk}\) ab \(y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}\) / y... Nothing \(\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{j=1}^{b}\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_{ijk}\) abn The forms that retain k are valid sums, but a replicate number alone does not automatically represent a common block, time, or matched subject across cells. Give k that interpretation only when the experimental design supports it.

sections.heading: A bar changes a total into a mean
breadcrumb: Understanding Dot Notation in Plain English
Three indices: factor A, factor B, and replicate
A bar changes a total into a mean
sections.text: In this lesson, an unbarred y with dots is a total ; a bar indicates a mean . Dots tell you which positions were aggregated. The bar tells you that division by the number of included observations is also required. \[\bar y_{ij\cdot}=\frac{y_{ij\cdot}}{n},\qquad \bar y_{i\cdot\cdot}=\frac{y_{i\cdot\cdot}}{bn}\] \[\bar y_{\cdot j\cdot}=\frac{y_{\cdot j\cdot}}{an},\qquad \bar y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}=\frac{y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}}{abn}\] Read the author's definitions: notation conventions vary. A dot is not itself an instruction to average. With unequal cell sizes, use the actual number of observations in each total; the balanced-design denominators above no longer apply unchanged.

sections.heading: Dot notation versus the summation sign
breadcrumb: Understanding Dot Notation in Plain English
Dot notation versus the summation sign
sections.text: Dot notation names an aggregated quantity. The summation sign \(\sum\) writes out the addition operation. They can represent exactly the same total; they are not competing statistical methods. \[y_{\cdot j\cdot}=\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_{ijk}\] On the left, two dots say which indices have been summed out. On the right, the two summation signs explicitly give their indices and limits. The j remains fixed on both sides. Use dot notation when… Use a summation sign when… Referring repeatedly to a row, column, cell, or grand total. Showing precisely which values to add and their bounds. Keeping a statistical formula compact. Adding transformed terms, such as squares, residuals, or chi-square contributions. Showing the indices retained after aggregation. Deriving or implementing the calculation step by step.

sections.heading: Why one formula can contain both
breadcrumb: Understanding Dot Notation in Plain English
Dot notation versus the summation sign
Why one formula can contain both
sections.text: \[\sum_{j=1}^{b}y_{\cdot j\cdot}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{b}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_{ijk}\right)^2\] For a fixed j, add all values across i and k. Square that B-level total. Repeat for each j, then add those squared totals. The outer sum still has a job: the dot total retains j. By contrast, \(\sum_{i,j,k}y_{ijk}^{2}\) squares each individual observation before adding, and \(y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}^{2}\) squares the single grand total. These three operations generally give different results. Avoid summing an index twice: \(\sum_i y_{\cdot j\cdot}=a\,y_{\cdot j\cdot}\), because i is already absent from the total. This repeats the same value a times; it does not create a new marginal total.

Worked example: dot notation in two-factor ANOVA
sections.text: Use this small, synthetic strength dataset (arbitrary units). A represents two temperature settings; B represents two cooling settings. Each cell contains two independent experimental runs, so \(a=b=n=2\) and \(N=abn=8\). The purpose is to practise the notation, not recommend process settings. Two-factor data and marginal totals A level B1: k1, k2 B2: k1, k2 A-level total A1 8, 10 (cell total 18) 12, 14 (cell total 26) 44 A2 10, 12 (cell total 22) 18, 20 (cell total 38) 60 B-level totals 40 64 Grand total 104 \[y_{112}=10,\quad y_{12\cdot}=12+14=26\] \[y_{1\cdot\cdot}=8+10+12+14=44\] \[y_{\cdot2\cdot}=12+14+18+20=64\] Thus \(\bar y_{\cdot2\cdot}=64/(an)=64/4=16\), while \(\bar y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}=104/8=13\). The first is the mean at B2; the second is the mean of all eight measurements.

sections.heading: Reading the sums-of-squares formulas
breadcrumb: Understanding Dot Notation in Plain English
Worked example: dot notation in two-factor ANOVA
sections.text: For this balanced, replicated, fixed-effects two-factor model, define the correction factor \(C=y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}^{2}/(abn)=104^2/8=1352\). The raw sum of squared observations is \(8^2+10^2+12^2+14^2+10^2+12^2+18^2+20^2=1472\). \[SS_T=\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{j=1}^{b}\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_{ijk}^{2}-C=1472-1352=120\] \[SS_A=\frac{1}{bn}\sum_{i=1}^{a}y_{i\cdot\cdot}^{2}-C=\frac{44^2+60^2}{4}-1352=32\] \[SS_B=\frac{1}{an}\sum_{j=1}^{b}y_{\cdot j\cdot}^{2}-C=\frac{40^2+64^2}{4}-1352=72\] \[SS_{AB}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{a}\sum_{j=1}^{b}y_{ij\cdot}^{2}-C-SS_A-SS_B\] \[SS_{AB}=\frac{18^2+26^2+22^2+38^2}{2}-1352-32-72=8\] \[SS_E=SS_T-SS_A-SS_B-SS_{AB}=120-32-72-8=8\] Here T means total corrected variation , A and B are the main effects, AB is their interaction, and E is within-cell error. Check the result directly: every observation is one unit from its cell mean, so eight squared deviations of 1 give \(SS_E=8\). The correction factor removes the overall mean contribution; it is not an error correction or a chi-square continuity correction. ANOVA calculation check Source SS Degrees of freedom MS = SS / df F = effect MS / error MS A 32 a − 1 = 1 32 16 B 72 b − 1 = 1 72 36 A × B 8 (a − 1)(b − 1) = 1 8 4 Error 8 ab(n − 1) = 4 2 — Total 120 abn − 1 = 7 — — ANOVA compares variation between factor-level means with residual variation. The observed B2–B1 difference is 4 at A1 and 8 at A2: this difference of differences explains the nonzero interaction SS. Statistical significance requires the appropriate F distribution and degrees of freedom, not just comparing raw SS values. Model conditions: inference assumes independent errors, approximately normal errors, and common error variance. Replicates must be independent experimental units, not repeated readings treated as new runs. With n = 1 there is no within-cell error df for this full interaction model. Unequal cell sizes require a general linear model and an explicit choice of sums of squares. Model and decomposition reference: NIST: two-way ANOVA . The dataset and arithmetic here are original teaching examples.

sections.heading: Worked example: chi-square test of independence
breadcrumb: Understanding Dot Notation in Plain English
Worked example: chi-square test of independence
sections.text: Now the cells contain counts of items , not strength measurements. In this synthetic example, 100 independently sampled pipes are classified by production line and inspection result. Each pipe is counted once. Let \(O_{ij}\) be the observed count in row i and column j. Some books write \(n_{ij}\) instead. Observed inspection counts Line (i) Pass (j = 1) Fail (j = 2) Row total \(O_{i\cdot}\) Line 1 30 20 50 Line 2 45 5 50 Column total \(O_{\cdot j}\) 75 25 \(O_{\cdot\cdot}=100\) \[O_{i\cdot}=\sum_j O_{ij},\quad O_{\cdot j}=\sum_i O_{ij},\quad N=O_{\cdot\cdot}=\sum_i\sum_j O_{ij}\] The null hypothesis is that line and inspection result are independent. Under independence, each line would have the overall pass proportion, 75/100, and fail proportion, 25/100. Multiply the row size by these proportions to obtain expected counts: \[E_{ij}=\frac{O_{i\cdot}O_{\cdot j}}{O_{\cdot\cdot}}\] \[E_{11}=\frac{50(75)}{100}=37.5,\qquad E_{12}=\frac{50(25)}{100}=12.5\] Line 2 has the same row total, so its expected counts are also 37.5 and 12.5. Expected counts can be fractional. Their row totals, column totals, and grand total match those of the observed table. \[\chi^2=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{c}\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}\] \[\chi^2=\frac{(30-37.5)^2}{37.5}+\frac{(20-12.5)^2}{12.5}+\frac{(45-37.5)^2}{37.5}+\frac{(5-12.5)^2}{12.5}\] \[\chi^2=1.5+4.5+1.5+4.5=12,\qquad df=(r-1)(c-1)=1\] The uncorrected Pearson test gives p ≈ 0.000532. At α = 0.05, reject independence: there is evidence of an association between line and inspection result. This does not establish that the line caused the difference. Two jobs in one test: the dots provide marginal totals for the expected counts; the summation signs add the four cell contributions to the test statistic. Do not include the margins themselves as extra cells in that sum. Use nonnegative frequency counts, mutually exclusive categories, independent observations, and adequately large expected counts. All four expected counts here exceed 5. For sparse tables, consider a suitable exact method rather than relying on the chi-square approximation. This example uses no Yates continuity correction. Question ANOVA Chi-square independence What is recorded? A numerical response for each experimental unit A count for each pair of categories What do dots summarize? Response totals or, with a bar, means Row counts, column counts, and sample size What does Σ combine? Squared totals or squared deviations, as the formula specifies Standardized squared observed–expected differences What is tested? Mean effects and interaction in the specified model Association between two categorical variables Method and implementation references: Microsoft: CHISQ.TEST and Minitab: table analyses .

sections.text: ANOVA data: enter the four A–B cells as rows 2–5, with the two replicate values in B:C: (8,10), (12,14), (10,12), (18,20). Put =SUM(B2:C2) in D2 and fill to D5. Then: Cell total: D2 = 18; cell mean: =AVERAGE(B2:C2) = 9. A1 total: =SUM(D2:D3) = 44; B2 total: =SUM(D3,D5) = 64. Grand total: =SUM(B2:C5) = 104; raw sum of squares: =SUMSQ(B2:C5) = 1472. Total SS: =SUMSQ(B2:C5)-SUM(B2:C5)^2/8 = 120. Sum of squared cell totals: =SUMSQ(D2:D5) = 2928. These inputs are already totals, unlike the raw observations in B:C. Interaction p-value: =F.DIST.RT(4,1,4) ≈ 0.1161. The nonzero observed interaction is not statistically significant at 0.05 in this tiny example. Chi-square data, on a separate sheet: place 30,20 in B2:C2 and 45,5 in B3:C3. Row totals go in D2:D3, column totals in B4:C4, and the grand total in D4. Put =$D2*B$4/$D$4 in F2, then fill across to G2 and down to row 3. Expected counts in F2:G3 are 37.5,12.5 in both rows. Statistic: =SUMPRODUCT((B2:C3-F2:G3)^2/F2:G3) = 12. P-value: =CHISQ.TEST(B2:C3,F2:G3) ≈ 0.000532. Check: =CHISQ.DIST.RT(12,1) gives the same p-value. Exclude totals from the test ranges. CHISQ.TEST returns a p-value, not the statistic 12. These references assume the exact layouts above and no missing observations.

sections.heading: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
sections.text: Understand what is changing, how fast it changes, and how much accumulates. Calculus connects a process curve to decisions: how sensitive a response is to temperature, how defects accumulate during a shift, and how failure probabilities change with time. This lesson starts with the ideas, builds the rules, then applies them to engineering. Download formula cheat sheet (PDF) By the end, you can: interpret a slope and an integral; select product, quotient and chain rules; use substitution and integration by parts; calculate a definite integral; and connect failure density, reliability and hazard. Before you begin: be comfortable with fractions, powers, function notation and basic algebra. All engineering numbers here are teaching examples, not production predictions.

An indefinite integral gives a family of antiderivatives. A definite integral gives a number for an interval: ∫ 0 3 2 x d x = 9 \displaystyle \int_{0}^{3} 2x dx = 9 . What about fractions and square roots?
sections.text: There is no general integration quotient rule. For rational functions, algebra or partial fractions may help: 1 [ x ( x + 1 ) ] = 1 x − 1 x + 1 \displaystyle \frac{1}{[x(x + 1)]} = \frac{1}{x }- \frac{1}{x + 1} . Integrate the pieces to get ln|x| − ln|x + 1| + C. Trigonometric substitution can simplify roots: for a 2 − x 2 \displaystyle \sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} , use x = a sin ⁡ θ \displaystyle x = a \sin \theta with a suitable angle interval, then d x = a cos ⁡ θ d θ \displaystyle dx = a \cos \theta d\theta . These are pattern-based methods; numerical integration handles many cases without simple antiderivatives.

sections.text: Split [a,b] into n intervals of width Δ x = ( b − a ) n \displaystyle \Delta x = \frac{(b - a)}{n} . A rectangle has height f ( x i ) \displaystyle f(x_i) and area f ( x i ) Δ x \displaystyle f(x_i)\Delta x . Adding the rectangles estimates the integral. For a continuous curve, the estimates converge as the largest interval width approaches zero. We use a limit; we do not literally calculate an infinite number of rectangles.

sections.heading: 06 / Calculus in quality and reliability
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
sections.text: In quality, area under a continuous measurement density between specification limits gives the conforming probability. In reliability, the variable is time to failure T. The same slope-and-area ideas connect four quantities: Quantity Meaning Units F ( t ) \displaystyle F(t) Probability of failure by t Dimensionless R ( t ) = 1 − F ( t ) \displaystyle R(t) = 1 - F(t) Probability of surviving beyond t Dimensionless f ( t ) = F ′ ( t ) = − R ′ ( t ) \displaystyle f(t)=F'(t)=-R'(t) Failure-time density; integrate it for probability inverse time h ( t ) = f ( t ) R ( t ) \displaystyle h(t) = \frac{f(t)}{R(t)} Instantaneous failure rate among survivors inverse time For continuous lifetimes, P( T = t ) \displaystyle T = t) is zero; f ( t ) \displaystyle f(t) is a density, not a point probability. Hazard is also not a probability. Over a short Δ t , h ( t ) Δ t \displaystyle \Delta t, h(t)\Delta t approximates the conditional probability of failure, given survival to t.

sections.heading: Live lab: exponential reliability
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
sections.text: The exponential model assumes constant hazard λ, as described in the NIST handbook . Its survival curve is R ( t ) = e − λ t \displaystyle R(t) = e^{-\lambda t} , with time in hours and λ per hour. Raise λ and watch survival drop faster. The shaded area under the density from 0 to t is F ( t ) \displaystyle F(t) . Hazard λ (per hour) Time t (hours) At λ = 0.002 h \displaystyle \lambda = \frac{0.002}{h} and t = 100 h \displaystyle t = 100 h , reliability is 81.87% and failure probability is 18.13%. sections.text: Differentiate R ( t ) = e − λ t \displaystyle R(t) = e^{-\lambda t} using the chain rule: R ′ ( t ) = − λ e − λ t \displaystyle R'(t) = -\lambda e^{-\lambda t} . Therefore f ( t ) = − R ′ ( t ) = λ e − λ t \displaystyle f(t) = -R'(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t} . Divide f ( t ) \displaystyle f(t) by R ( t ) \displaystyle R(t) to recover h ( t ) = λ \displaystyle h(t) = \lambda . Integrating f from 0 to t gives 1 − e − λ t \displaystyle 1 - e^{-\lambda t} . Integrating R from 0 to infinity gives M T T F = 1 λ \displaystyle MTTF = \frac{1}{\lambda } . For a changing hazard, use H ( t ) = ∫ 0 t h \displaystyle H(t) = \int_{0}^{t} h (s)ds and R ( t ) = exp ⁡ [ − H ( t ) ] \displaystyle R(t) = \exp [-H(t)] , assuming R ( 0 ) = 1 \displaystyle R(0) = 1 . Do not force a constant-hazard model onto wear-out or early-life failure patterns. MTTF describes a lifetime model; it is not automatically the MTBF of a repaired system.

Here F ( t ) = P ( T ≤ t ) \displaystyle F(t)=P(T\leq t) is dimensionless, while f ( t ) \displaystyle f(t) has units of inverse time. The model has F ( 0 ) = 0 \displaystyle F(0)=0 and zero density for negative time.

sections.heading: A. Differentiate the CDF to obtain the PDF
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
Worked example: differentiation and integration go both ways
A. Differentiate the CDF to obtain the PDF
sections.text: Step 1 — Write the relationship and substitute the CDF. The density is the derivative of cumulative probability. f ( t ) = d F ( t ) d t = d d t ( 1 − e − λ t ) \displaystyle f(t)=\frac{dF(t)}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right) Step 2 — Differentiate each term. The derivative of the constant one is zero. Keep the subtraction sign in front of the exponential. f ( t ) = d d t ( 1 ) − d d t ( e − λ t ) = 0 − d d t ( e − λ t ) \displaystyle f(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(1)-\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-\lambda t}\right)=0-\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-\lambda t}\right) Step 3 — Identify the inner function. The outer function is the exponential. The exponent is the inner function; its derivative is the negative constant hazard. g ( t ) = − λ t , g ′ ( t ) = − λ \displaystyle g(t)=-\lambda t,\qquad g^{\prime}(t)=-\lambda d d t e g ( t ) = e g ( t ) g ′ ( t ) \displaystyle \frac{d}{dt}e^{g(t)}=e^{g(t)}g^{\prime}(t) d d t e − λ t = e − λ t ( − λ ) = − λ e − λ t \displaystyle \frac{d}{dt}e^{-\lambda t}=e^{-\lambda t}(-\lambda)=-\lambda e^{-\lambda t} Step 4 — Substitute and simplify both minus signs. One minus comes from the CDF’s subtraction; the other comes from differentiating the exponent. f ( t ) = 0 − ( − λ e − λ t ) = 0 + λ e − λ t = λ e − λ t \displaystyle f(t)=0-\left(-\lambda e^{-\lambda t}\right)=0+\lambda e^{-\lambda t}=\boxed{\lambda e^{-\lambda t}} Interpretation. The slope of the CDF at a selected time is the height of the density at that time. The density is nonnegative, so the CDF never decreases.

sections.heading: B. Integrate the PDF to recover the CDF
breadcrumb: Introduction to Calculus for Quality and Reliability Engineers
Worked example: differentiation and integration go both ways
B. Integrate the PDF to recover the CDF
sections.text: Step 1 — Set up the accumulated probability. Use u \displaystyle u as the integration variable so that t \displaystyle t remains the fixed upper endpoint. The lower bound is zero because this model has no negative failure times and no probability mass at zero. F ( t ) = ∫ 0 t f ( u ) d u = ∫ 0 t λ e − λ u d u \displaystyle F(t)=\int_0^t f(u)\,du=\int_0^t\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du Step 2 — Find an antiderivative by substitution. Replace the exponent with a simpler variable. Solve explicitly for the differential. w = − λ u \displaystyle w=-\lambda u d w d u = − λ , d w = − λ d u , d u = − 1 λ d w \displaystyle \frac{dw}{du}=-\lambda,\qquad dw=-\lambda\,du,\qquad du=-\frac{1}{\lambda}\,dw Step 3 — Substitute both the exponential and the differential. The constant hazard cancels its reciprocal. The minus sign remains. ∫ λ e − λ u d u = ∫ λ e w ( − 1 λ ) d w \displaystyle \int\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du=\int\lambda e^w\left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right)\,dw = − ∫ e w d w = − e w + C \displaystyle = -\int e^w\,dw=-e^w+C Step 4 — Return to the original integration variable. ∫ λ e − λ u d u = − e − λ u + C \displaystyle \int\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du=-e^{-\lambda u}+C Step 5 — Evaluate upper endpoint minus lower endpoint. Use the antiderivative at each bound. The same constant cancels. F ( t ) = [ − e − λ u ] 0 t \displaystyle F(t)=\left[-e^{-\lambda u}\right]_0^t = ( − e − λ t + C ) − ( − e − λ ⋅ 0 + C ) \displaystyle =\left(-e^{-\lambda t}+C\right)-\left(-e^{-\lambda\cdot0}+C\right) = − e − λ t + e 0 = − e − λ t + 1 = 1 − e − λ t \displaystyle =-e^{-\lambda t}+e^0=-e^{-\lambda t}+1=\boxed{1-e^{-\lambda t}} Alternative: change the bounds during substitution. If you keep the new variable throughout, transform both limits. This gives the same result without substituting back. u = 0 ⇒ w = 0 , u = t ⇒ w = − λ t \displaystyle u=0\Rightarrow w=0,\qquad u=t\Rightarrow w=-\lambda t F ( t ) = − ∫ 0 − λ t e w d w = − [ e w ] 0 − λ t = − ( e − λ t − 1 ) = 1 − e − λ t \displaystyle F(t)=-\int_0^{-\lambda t}e^w\,dw=-\left[e^w\right]_0^{-\lambda t}=-(e^{-\lambda t}-1)=1-e^{-\lambda t}
